name: Grade 11
theme: The sacraments and the moral life in Christ

lessons.title: Christ’s work in the liturgy
lessons.idea: The liturgy is the work of Christ the High Priest and of his Body, the Church. In it God sanctifies us and we worship him; it is the source and summit of the Church’s life. Jesus said true worshipers will worship “in spirit and truth.”
lessons.question: Why is liturgy more than a ritual?
lessons.activity: “Study Sacrosanctum Concilium 7” (40 min). Students read SC 7 and annotate: Christ present in the Mass (minister, species, word, community), the liturgy as the exercise of Christ’s priesthood, the foretaste of heavenly liturgy. Write a paragraph explaining why liturgy is more than ceremony. Read John 4:21–24.
teach: “The liturgy is the participation of the People of God in ‘the work of God’” (CCC 1069). It is the exercise of Christ’s priestly office, in which sanctification is manifested by signs and worship is offered by the whole Body (CCC 1070–1073; SC 7).
Christ is present in the Eucharistic species, in the priest, in the Word, in the gathered community, and in the sacraments (CCC 1088; SC 7).

The liturgy is also the anticipation of the heavenly liturgy (Revelation 4–5; CCC 1090). The Trinity is at work: the Father is source and goal, the Son the mediator, the Spirit prepares and makes present (CCC 1077–1112).
Full, conscious, active participation is the goal (CCC 1071; SC 14).
talk: What does “work of the people” mean?
Why is liturgy more than ritual?
quiz: Sacrosanctum Concilium 7 lists several ways Christ is present in the liturgy. Which is NOT among them?|Only in the tabernacle outside Mass|In the Word proclaimed|In the person of the minister|In the Eucharistic species|0|CCC 1088: minister, species, word, assembly; the tabernacle is a real presence too but not the only one.
“Liturgy” (leitourgia) originally meant…|A silent prayer|A public work done for the people|A feast day|A private devotion|1|CCC 1069.

Why is the liturgy called “source and summit”?|All the Church’s activity flows from it and is directed to it (CCC 1074)|It is the longest prayer|It is for clergy only|It is the oldest rite|0|CCC 1074; SC 10.
lessons.life: Read Sacrosanctum Concilium 7 and 10.
lessons.saint: Hippolytus of Rome: a priest and writer who recorded how the Church prayed in the early 200s.
lessons.mem: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.” (John 4:24)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What does ‘liturgy’ mean?” Greek leitourgia, “public work.” “Whose work is it?” Explore the answer: Christ’s, and ours with him.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how Christ is present in the liturgy in five ways.

script.open: Read aloud the opening dialogue of the Eucharistic Prayer from the Missal, back and forth with the class. Ask, “How old do you think these words are? Who is speaking, and to whom?”
teach: Say: “The word ‘liturgy’ comes from the Greek leitourgia, ‘public work’ or ‘service of the people.’ In the Church it means the participation of the People of God in the work of God. Vatican II’s Sacrosanctum Concilium says that in the liturgy, ‘the work of our redemption is accomplished.’ (SC 2) Christ is always present in his Church, especially in her liturgical actions: in the person of the minister, in the Eucharistic species, in his word, and when the community prays and sings. (SC 7) So the liturgy is not a performance by the priest, or merely a human gathering. It is the work of Christ the High Priest, with his Body, the Church.”

Say: “The liturgy is the action of the whole Trinity. The Father is the source and goal: we bless him as Creator. The Son makes present the Paschal Mystery, his death and Resurrection; he is the priest and the sacrifice. The Holy Spirit prepares the Church to meet Christ, recalls the mystery to mind (anamnesis), makes it present, and unites us in communion. Look at the structure of the Eucharistic Prayer: we thank the Father (preface), we remember Christ’s saving work (anamnesis), we call down the Spirit (epiclesis) and we offer, intercede and glorify in the doxology: ‘Through him, and with him, and in him.’”

Say: “The liturgy also anticipates heaven. Revelation 4-5 pictures the heavenly liturgy: the Lamb, the elders, the angels, the song ‘Holy, holy, holy.’ In the Mass we join this. The Church year unfolds the mystery of Christ: Advent, Christmas, Lent, the Triduum, Easter, Ordinary Time. The Easter Vigil is the ‘mother of all vigils.’ Vatican II also taught that the liturgy is ‘the summit toward which the activity of the Church is directed; it is also the font from which all her power flows.’ (SC 10) Hence the call for ‘full, conscious and active participation’ (SC 14): not just doing things but offering ourselves with Christ. Hippolytus’s text shows this is ancient.”
ask: What does ‘liturgy’ mean? (Public work or service of the people.)
Who is the principal agent of the liturgy? (Christ, the High Priest, with his Body the Church.)
What are the roles of the Trinity in the liturgy? (Father is source, Son makes present the Paschal Mystery, Spirit prepares and unites.)
practice: Read the Eucharistic Prayer’s preface dialogue and mark who speaks each line.
Make a chart: Father, Son, Holy Spirit. Under each, find where they are named or acted in the Eucharistic Prayer.
Identify four moments where the Mass echoes Revelation 4-5.
Write a sentence: “At Mass, the real actor is…”
script.close: Pray the preface dialogue together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pay attention to the words ‘Lift up your hearts’ at Mass.”

tryit: Read the opening dialogue of the Eucharistic Prayer.
Mark who speaks.
Say whose action the liturgy is.
lessons.saintStory:
Hippolytus was a priest and teacher in Rome in the early third century, a learned man who wrote on many subjects. He disagreed with several popes, was elected a rival bishop of Rome by his followers, and spent years outside the main body of the Church. During the persecution under Emperor Maximinus Thrax, around 235, he and Pope Pontian were both exiled to the mines of Sardinia. There they were reconciled, and both died of the hardships.
His best-known work, the Apostolic Tradition, describes how the Roman Church worshiped: the ordination of bishops, priests and deacons, the preparation and Baptism of converts, and a Eucharistic Prayer. It begins with a dialogue still used today: “The Lord be with you. And with your spirit. Lift up your hearts. We lift them up to the Lord. Let us give thanks to the Lord. It is right and just.”
The Church honors him as a martyr and a witness to the liturgy. His text shows how much of the Mass we pray today goes back to the early Church.

lessons.title: Signs that give grace
lessons.idea: Sacraments are efficacious signs of grace instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church. Each uses matter and form, and works ex opere operato: by the power of Christ’s action, not the minister’s holiness. They continue Jesus’ touching and healing in the Gospels.
lessons.question: What does “ex opere operato” mean?
lessons.activity: “Matter and form chart” (35 min). Students create a chart for the seven sacraments: matter, form, minister, effect. Identify the “visible sign” and “invisible grace.” Include sacramentals as distinct. Discuss why God works through material things.
teach: “Sacraments are efficacious signs of grace, instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church” (CCC 1131). They “make present” what they signify (CCC 1084).
Ex opere operato: the sacrament works by the very fact of the action’s being performed (CCC 1128). This protects us from the minister’s unworthiness; the fruit depends on the recipient’s disposition.
Matter and form come from the early Church’s theology; matter is the thing (water, oil), form the words. The minister must intend what the Church does (CCC 1256, 1584).
Sacramentals (blessings, holy water, medals) are sacred signs instituted by the Church that prepare us for grace (CCC 1667–1679).
talk: What does ex opere operato protect?
quiz: Ex opere operato means that a sacrament…|Is magic|Requires no faith to bear fruit|Acts by Christ’s power when rightly celebrated, apart from the minister’s personal holiness (CCC 1128)|Works because the minister is holy|2|CCC 1127–1128.
The sign of a sacrament consists of…|Only intention|Only gestures|Only words|Matter and form (things and words)|3|CCC 1084, 1131.
Which is a sacramental rather than a sacrament?|Holy water|Anointing|Marriage|Baptism|0|CCC 1667–1673.
lessons.life: Chart matter, form and minister for the seven sacraments.
lessons.saint: Martin of Tours: a soldier who cut his cloak for a beggar and saw Christ wearing it.
lessons.mem: “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.” (Mark 5:34)
lessons.hook: Read Mark 5:25–34, the woman who touches Jesus’ cloak. Ask: “What went out from Jesus?” Sacraments are touch points of his power.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain ex opere operato and complete a matter/form chart for three sacraments.

script.open: Hold up a plain cup of water and say, “This is water. Now suppose a priest pours it on a child’s head and says certain words. What do Catholics say happens? What is the difference between the water in my cup and the water at the font?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “A sacrament is ‘an efficacious sign of grace, instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church, by which divine life is dispensed to us.’ (CCC 1131) ‘Sign’ because it is something visible that points to something invisible. ‘Efficacious’ because it actually accomplishes what it signifies. ‘Instituted by Christ’ because only he can attach grace to a sign. ‘Entrusted to the Church’ because she celebrates and dispenses them. The Church has always recognized seven: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance, Anointing, Holy Orders, Matrimony. The Council of Trent defined that there are seven, and not more or fewer, and that all were instituted by Christ.”

Say: “Each sacrament has matter and form. The matter is the material element or action (water, bread and wine, oil, laying on of hands, the exchange of consent). The form is the words that give the matter its meaning (‘I baptize you in the name of the Father…’). Together they make the sign. The minister: usually a bishop, priest or deacon, but the spouses are ministers of Matrimony, and anyone may baptize in an emergency. The minister must have the intention of doing what the Church does. If any essential part is missing, the sacrament is invalid. For instance, baptizing with juice instead of water, or changing the Trinitarian formula, does not baptize.”

Say: “How do sacraments work? The Church speaks of ex opere operato, ‘by the work done.’ The sacrament confers grace by the very fact of the action being performed, because Christ is acting, and not because of the personal holiness of the minister. A priest in a state of sin still validly consecrates the Eucharist and forgives sins. This protects us: we don’t depend on the minister’s worthiness. But the fruit received depends on our disposition. Three sacraments (Baptism, Confirmation, Holy Orders) confer a character, an indelible spiritual mark; they can’t be repeated. The sacraments are ‘sacraments of faith’: they presuppose, nourish and express faith. Aquinas called them ‘signs that cause what they signify.’”
ask: What is a sacrament? (An efficacious sign of grace, instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church.)
What are matter and form? (The material element and the words.)
What does ex opere operato mean? (The sacrament works by Christ’s action, not the minister’s holiness.)
practice: Make a table of the seven sacraments with columns: matter, form, minister, effect.
Fill in as much as you can, then check with the Catechism.
Mark the three that confer a character.
Choose one and write what would make it invalid.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, you meet us in visible signs. Give us faith to see.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look for the sign in each sacrament you see this month.”

tryit: Analyze one sacrament as matter, form, minister and effect.
Test whether each part is necessary.
Say what the sign shows.
lessons.saintStory:
Martin was born around 316 in what is now Hungary, the son of a Roman officer. He was enrolled in the army at fifteen, and posted in Gaul. He was a catechumen, someone preparing for Baptism, though he had not yet been baptized. One winter day, at the gates of Amiens, he met a beggar who was nearly naked and shivering. Martin had nothing but his weapons and his cloak. He drew his sword, cut the cloak in two and gave half to the man.
That night he dreamed of Christ wearing the half-cloak, saying to the angels, “Martin, who is still a catechumen, has clothed me.” Martin was baptized soon after, and left the army, saying, “I am a soldier of Christ; I am not allowed to fight.” He became a disciple of Hilary of Poitiers, a monk, and in 371 the bishop of Tours, where he lived simply in a cell, and traveled to bring the Gospel to rural people.
He died in 397. The half-cloak, or cappa, was kept as a relic, giving the word “chapel.” His act shows how a visible sign can carry an invisible reality.

lessons.title: Disposition and fruitfulness
lessons.idea: Sacraments bear fruit according to the faith and disposition of those who receive them. Faith, repentance and desire open us to grace, while indifference or insincerity can block it. Preparation and thanksgiving matter.
lessons.question: Why are dispositions important?
lessons.activity: “Reflect on your reception” (35 min). Students privately reflect on the last time they received a sacrament: How did I prepare? How attentive was I? How did it change me? Write a short plan for a deeper reception. No sharing required, only volunteers.
teach: The sacraments confer grace, but it bears fruit according to dispositions (CCC 1128, 1131). Faith is required: they are “sacraments of faith” (CCC 1122–1126).
Hebrews 11:6: “without faith it is impossible to please him.” Repentance is needed for Eucharist and Confirmation if in mortal sin (CCC 1415).
Obstacles: unrepented mortal sin, indifference, a faithless approach. Fruits increase with devotion, as with spiritual preparation (CCC 1123–1126).
Sacramental life is the normal means of spiritual growth, but God’s grace is not limited to them (CCC 1257).
talk: What is the role of faith?
How can we participate more fully?
quiz: Why can two people receive the same sacrament with different fruit?|Fruit depends on the recipient’s faith and dispositions (CCC 1128)|One minister is better|The sacrament changes|It is random|0|CCC 1128.

Hebrews 11:6 says “without faith it is impossible to please” God. In sacramental theology this stresses that…|Only adults receive grace|Sacraments are sacraments of faith, and faith opens us to grace|Doubt invalidates them|Faith is optional|1|CCC 1123.
A person in mortal sin who approaches Communion should first…|Go to Confession (CCC 1385)|Receive anyway|Fast two days|Do nothing|0|CCC 1385, 1415.
lessons.life: Prepare for the next Mass by praying the readings beforehand.
lessons.saint: Stanislaus Kostka: a Polish teenager who walked to Rome to become a Jesuit and received Communion with extraordinary devotion.
misc: “The sacraments work regardless of my attitude.”
“I must be perfect before I receive.”
lessons.mem: “And without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.” (Hebrews 11:6)
lessons.hook: Hold out a gift and ask a volunteer to receive it with arms crossed. “The gift is real but is it received?” Introduce disposition.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how disposition affects sacramental fruit and give an example.

script.open: Ask, “Two people attend the same Mass. One leaves unchanged; the other is moved. What might account for the difference?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Sacraments work ex opere operato, but they do not work like magic. The fruit received depends on the disposition of the recipient. The Catechism: ‘The fruits of the sacraments also depend on the disposition of the one who receives them.’ (CCC 1128) Disposition means the state of heart and mind: faith, repentance, openness, the intention to receive what the Church gives. A sacrament received validly but without proper disposition may be valid, but its fruits are blocked, until the obstacle is removed. For example, a person who is baptized as an adult without any intention of repenting; the character is imprinted, but the grace awaits.”

Say: “Obstacles. Mortal sin: a person who receives Communion in mortal sin commits sacrilege (1 Corinthians 11:27-29), and must first be reconciled in Confession. Lack of faith or intention. Hypocrisy, holding a grudge, or hidden hostility. Distraction and routine, which won’t invalidate but diminish. What helps: prayer before and after; examination of conscience; fasting; recollection; asking the Spirit’s help; making the effort to come early; confessing sins; reconciling with those we’ve wronged; and thanksgiving. We can compare it to sunlight on a window: the sun shines, but a dirty window keeps out the light.”

Say: “Sacraments are also fruitful in time. The grace given in Baptism or Confirmation can ‘revive’ when a person later repents (reviviscence). The seeds of grace need cultivation. Sacraments also have effects that are ecclesial: they build the Church. Receiving the Eucharist unworthily harms not just oneself but the community. Remember the parable of the sower. The word is the same, the seed is the same; the soil determines the yield. Pope Pius X’s encouragement of frequent Communion came with the condition of right intention and state of grace. And Stanislaus prepared with great fervor. We should treat the sacraments not as routine but as encounters with Christ.”
ask: Do sacraments work like magic? (No; fruit depends on our disposition.)
What is an obstacle to the fruit? (Mortal sin, lack of faith, hypocrisy, distraction.)
What helps? (Prayer, examination, Confession, reconciliation, thanksgiving.)
practice: Make two lists: obstacles and helps for receiving Communion fruitfully.
Write a 5-step routine for preparing for Mass (night before, morning, arriving, during, after).
Mark which step you most often skip.
Commit to one change this month.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, make my heart a good soil.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Prepare for Mass for five minutes before leaving home.”

tryit: List obstacles to the fruit of a sacrament.
List what helps it.
Write your preparation plan.
lessons.saintStory:
Stanislaus Kostka was born in 1550 into a noble Polish family. At fourteen, he and his older brother Paul were sent to study in Vienna, at a Jesuit school. Stanislaus was serious about his faith, which his brother mocked. When he fell dangerously ill, the Lutheran family where he lodged would not allow a priest to bring him the Eucharist. Stanislaus is said to have prayed to St. Barbara, patron of the dying, and an angel brought him Communion. Recovered, he was determined to become a Jesuit.
The Austrian Jesuits could not accept him without his father’s permission, which they knew he would not give. So Stanislaus left Vienna in disguise, and walked about 350 miles to Augsburg and then to Rome, where the superior general, Francis Borgia, accepted him in 1567.
He lived as a novice for only ten months. He died in August 1568, at seventeen, after a short illness. He is the patron of students and novices, and shows what a heart disposed for the sacraments is like.

lessons.title: Baptism
lessons.idea: Baptism is new birth in water and the Spirit. Its matter is water; its form, “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” It forgives original and personal sin, makes us children of God and incorporates us into the Church. Infants are baptized; those who die before Baptism can be saved by desire or blood.
lessons.question: Why baptize infants?
lessons.activity: “Rite and objections” (40 min). Students study the Rite of Baptism and then prepare answers to: “Why baptize infants?”, “Isn’t it just symbolic?”, “What about the unbaptized?” Use CCC 1213–1284 and Scripture (Acts 16:15, 33; Colossians 2:11–12).
teach: Baptism is the “gateway to life in the Spirit” and the door to the other sacraments (CCC 1213). Its effects: forgiveness of sin, new birth, incorporation into Christ and the Church, an indelible character (CCC 1262–1274).
Minister: bishop, priest, deacon; in necessity anyone with the right intention (CCC 1256). Baptism by water is ordinary; baptism of blood (martyrdom) and desire also bring salvation (CCC 1258–1260).
Infant Baptism: the Church has done so since apostolic times; it rests on the gratuity of grace (CCC 1250–1252).
The Church entrusts unbaptized infants to God’s mercy (CCC 1261).
quiz: Baptism of desire applies to…|Anyone who ignores the Church|None|Infants only|Those who seek God and would be baptized if they knew (CCC 1258–1260)|3|CCC 1259.

The ordinary ministers of Baptism are…|Bishops, priests and deacons, though anyone may baptize in necessity with water and the Trinitarian formula (CCC 1256)|Only priests|Godparents|Only bishops|0|CCC 1256.

A good reply to “infants should not be baptized because they cannot choose” is that…|Parents decide everything|Choice is irrelevant|Grace is a gift offered to the child, as with other gifts parents give; the Church has baptized households from apostolic times (CCC 1250–1252)|The question is wrong|2|CCC 1250–1252; Acts 16:15.
lessons.life: Read the Rite of Baptism.
lessons.saint: Remigius of Reims: the bishop who baptized Clovis and the Franks.
misc: “Infants are baptized without their consent, so it’s invalid.”
“Baptism guarantees heaven regardless of how you live.”
lessons.mem: “Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” (John 3:5)
lessons.hook: Read John 3:1–8. Ask: “Why did Nicodemus misunderstand ‘born again’?” Compare to Baptism.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the effects of Baptism and defend infant Baptism.

script.open: Ask, “If Baptism only washed away original sin, why would the early Church baptize at Easter with a whole night of preparation? What else is happening?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Baptism is the first of the sacraments, the ‘door’ to life in the Spirit. It is necessary for salvation (John 3:5, ‘unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God’). The Catechism lists its effects. One: forgiveness of all sin, original sin and personal sins, and all punishment for sin. Two: new birth as children of God, sharing in the divine nature, members of Christ and temples of the Spirit. Three: incorporation into the Church, the Body of Christ. Four: an indelible spiritual character, a permanent sign of belonging to Christ. Five: the theological virtues and gifts of the Spirit. After Baptism a person still has concupiscence (inclination to sin), a struggle that continues.”

Say: “The rite. The sign is water, either by immersion or pouring, with the Trinitarian formula. The rite includes: reception of the child, the Sign of the Cross, liturgy of the Word, the exorcism and anointing with the oil of catechumens, the blessing of the water, the renunciation of sin and profession of faith, the baptism itself, the anointing with chrism, the white garment, the lighted candle from the Easter candle, the Our Father, and the blessing. For adults, the rite of Christian initiation includes the catechumenate, the scrutinies in Lent, and baptism at the Easter Vigil, together with Confirmation and Eucharist. Each sign has biblical roots: water (creation, flood, Red Sea, Jordan), oil (anointing), white garment (Galatians 3:27, ‘put on Christ’).”

Say: “Questions. Infant Baptism: the Church baptizes infants because it is a gift of grace, not a reward; parents and godparents promise to raise the child in the faith. The early Church practiced it (Origen says it comes from the apostles). Where an infant dies unbaptized, the Church entrusts to God’s mercy. Emergency Baptism: anyone may baptize with water and the right words and intention. Baptism of desire and blood. Baptism in other Christian churches is recognized. Who may be a godparent: a confirmed Catholic in good standing, at least sixteen. Why one name: Baptism gives each a Christian name. The Church ministers: bishop, priest, deacon. Baptism isn’t just a ceremony but a death and rising with Christ.”
ask: Name three effects of Baptism. (Forgiveness of sin, new birth as God’s child, incorporation into the Church.)
What is the character? (An indelible spiritual mark.)
Who may baptize in an emergency? (Anyone with water, the Trinitarian formula and the right intention.)
practice: Match each rite element to its meaning and Bible text in a table.
Write a short answer to a Protestant friend who says infant Baptism isn’t biblical.
Find your own baptismal date, parish and godparents.
Write a thank-you note to your godparent.
script.close: Renew your baptismal promises. Sign of the Cross with holy water. Send home: “Thank your godparents.”

tryit: Trace the effects of Baptism in the Catechism.
Match each to the rite.
Answer a skeptic on infant Baptism.
lessons.saintStory:
Remigius was born around 437 in what is now France, and became bishop of Reims at about twenty-two. He lived through the collapse of Roman rule in Gaul and the arrival of the Franks, a pagan Germanic people. In 481, Clovis became king of the Franks at fifteen. Clovis married Clotilde, a Catholic princess, who prayed for his conversion. During a battle against the Alemanni in 496, Clovis, seeing defeat, vowed that if the God of Clotilde gave him victory, he would be baptized.
He won, and on Christmas Day, about 496, Remigius baptized Clovis and, it is said, three thousand of his warriors. According to tradition, Remigius told him, “Bow your head, proud Sicambrian. Burn what you have worshiped, worship what you have burned.”
The baptism of Clovis led to the conversion of the Franks and a Catholic France. Remigius died around 533. Whether or not Clovis was fully converted in heart, the story shows how Baptism is a decisive entry into the Church.

lessons.title: Confirmation
lessons.idea: Confirmation completes baptismal grace by sealing us with the Holy Spirit. The bishop lays on hands and anoints with chrism, saying “Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.” We receive an increase of the Spirit’s gifts and a call to witness.
lessons.question: What do we receive?
lessons.activity: “Write a reflection” (35 min). Students write a reflection on the meaning of chrism (olive oil and balsam, consecrated by the bishop on Holy Thursday), the gifts, and their own call to witness. They answer: “What would it look like to live as sealed by the Spirit?”
teach: Confirmation, with Baptism and Eucharist, is a sacrament of initiation (CCC 1285). The rite includes renewal of baptismal promises, laying on of hands and anointing (CCC 1297–1301).

It imprints an indelible character and increases the gifts of the Spirit (CCC 1303–1305). The bishop is the original minister; priests confirm by delegation, especially in the Eastern Churches and in adult initiation (CCC 1312–1314).
Candidates must be baptized and in a state of grace; a sponsor helps (CCC 1306–1311).
Address the question of age: practice varies. The sacrament is not a “graduation” but a beginning of mission.
quiz: The essential rite of Confirmation is…|The bishop’s homily|The renewal of promises|A catechism test|Anointing with chrism with the laying on of hands and the words “Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit” (CCC 1300)|3|CCC 1300.
Confirmation imprints…|A civil record|A temporary seal|A lasting spiritual character, like Baptism and Holy Orders|Nothing|2|CCC 1304.

The Fathers and Eastern Churches differ from the Latin practice by…|Using no oil|Confirming infants right after Baptism through chrismation by the priest (CCC 1290, 1318)|Never confirming|Waiting till adulthood|1|CCC 1290, 1318.
lessons.life: Write a reflection on what the Spirit is calling you to.
lessons.saint: Chiara Luce Badano: a teenager who offered her illness for others and called it a gift.
misc: “Confirmation is only for those who choose it.”
“Confirmation gives gifts we did not already have at Baptism.”
lessons.mem: “Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.” (Rite of Confirmation)
lessons.hook: Read Acts 8:14–17. Ask: “What was missing after Philip’s baptisms? Why did Peter and John come?” Introduce the ancient practice of laying on of hands.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the rite, its effects and the role of the bishop.

script.open: Ask, “Confirmation is often called ‘the sacrament of Christian maturity.’ Is that accurate? What is it, if not graduation from religious ed?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Confirmation completes Baptism. The Catechism says: ‘By the sacrament of Confirmation, [the baptized] are more perfectly bound to the Church and are enriched with a special strength of the Holy Spirit. Hence they are, as true witnesses of Christ, more strictly obliged to spread and defend the faith by word and deed.’ (CCC 1285) The Scriptural basis: Pentecost (Acts 2), the laying on of hands at Samaria (Acts 8:14-17), at Ephesus (Acts 19:6). It is the sacrament of the gift of the Spirit. It deepens baptismal grace; roots us more deeply as God’s children; unites us more firmly to Christ; increases the gifts of the Spirit in us; makes our bond with the Church more perfect; and gives special strength to witness.”

Say: “The rite. The essential rite is the anointing with sacred chrism, accompanied by the laying on of the minister’s hand and the words, ‘Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.’ The chrism is olive oil mixed with balsam perfume, consecrated by the bishop at the Chrism Mass during Holy Week. The oil signifies strength, consecration and the fragrance of Christ. The Latin Church ordinarily gives Confirmation to those who have reached the age of discretion; the age varies, often ages 12-16 in the United States. The Eastern Churches confirm infants right after Baptism. The ordinary minister is the bishop. The candidate chooses a sponsor, a confirmed Catholic, and often a Confirmation name. The candidate renews baptismal promises.”

Say: “Confirmation’s place in the order of the sacraments of initiation (Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist) is debated. In the early Church, they were given together. In the Western Church, they were separated. Today Confirmation is sometimes given before First Communion in some dioceses, to restore the original order. For adults entering the Church, they are given together at the Easter Vigil. What does Confirmation ask of us? To be witnesses: of Christ in school, work and family. To use our gifts for the common good. To live as people of the Spirit: love, joy, peace and so on. Like Chiara, we receive the courage to say yes to God’s will.”
ask: What does Confirmation do? (Completes Baptism; gives strength to witness.)
What are the essential rite and words? (Anointing with chrism with the laying on of hands: ‘Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.’)
Who is the ordinary minister? (The bishop.)
practice: Draw a flowchart of the Confirmation rite with the meaning of each part.
Write about the saint you would choose as your Confirmation patron and why.
List three ways you will use the Spirit’s gifts to witness at school.
Write a prayer asking for the Holy Spirit.
script.close: Pray the prayer to the Holy Spirit. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray daily for the Spirit’s gifts.”

tryit: Read the rite of Confirmation.
Match each sign with its meaning.
Write your own preparation plan.
lessons.saintStory:
Chiara Badano was born in 1971 in northern Italy, after her parents had prayed for a child for eleven years. She loved sports, music and friends. At age nine she joined the Focolare Movement, which emphasizes unity and love. When she was seventeen, while playing tennis, she felt a sharp pain in her shoulder. She was diagnosed with bone cancer.
She was frightened, and for the first hours she said nothing. Then she said, “If you want it, Jesus, I want it too.” She accepted the treatment, refused morphine because it would dull her mind, saying she wanted to offer her pain to Jesus. Visitors came to cheer her up and left comforted themselves. She planned her funeral, choosing her dress, which she called her wedding gown, and the songs. She gave her corneas to a donor.
She died on October 7, 1990, at eighteen. Her last words to her mother: “Goodbye. Be happy, because I am.” She was beatified in 2010. She shows the courage that Confirmation gives.

lessons.title: Eucharist
lessons.idea: The Eucharist is the source and summit of the Christian life: institution at the Last Supper, Real Presence, sacrifice and banquet. John 6, Luke 22 and 1 Corinthians 11 are central texts. Christ gives himself under the appearances of bread and wine.
lessons.question: Why did Jesus say flesh?
lessons.activity: “Analyze John 6” (40 min). Students read John 6:22–71 and outline: the sign (bread), the discourse (bread from heaven, flesh and blood), the reaction. Compare with Luke 22:19–20 and 1 Corinthians 11:23–29. Write a one-page explanation of the Real Presence and how Scripture supports it.
teach: The Eucharist is “the source and summit of the Christian life” (CCC 1324). Institution: Last Supper (Luke 22; CCC 1337–1340).
The Real Presence: Christ is present “whole and entire… body and blood, soul and divinity” (CCC 1374). Transubstantiation names the change of substance (CCC 1376–1377).
The Eucharist is memorial, sacrifice, communion and thanksgiving (CCC 1356–1372). Fruits: union with Christ, forgiveness of venial sin, unity of the Church (CCC 1391–1397).
Paul warns that eating unworthily brings judgment (1 Corinthians 11:27–29). We prepare by faith, Confession as needed, fasting and reverence (CCC 1385–1387).
talk: Why did Jesus say flesh and blood?
How did early Christians treat the Eucharist?
quiz: In John 6, the crowd’s reaction to “my flesh is true food” shows that Jesus’ words were understood as…|A joke|A metaphor only|A parable|Literal enough that many left him (John 6:60–66)|3|John 6:66.

Transubstantiation names…|A symbolic remembrance|A change in appearance|A second sacrifice|The change of the whole substance of bread and wine into Christ’s Body and Blood while the appearances remain (CCC 1376)|3|CCC 1376.
The Mass is called a sacrifice because it…|Adds to it|Makes present the one sacrifice of Christ in an unbloody manner (CCC 1366–1367)|Repeats Calvary|Is only a meal|1|CCC 1366–1367; Hebrews 10:10.
lessons.life: Read Ignatius and Justin on the Eucharist.
lessons.saint: Paschal Baylon: a Spanish shepherd and Franciscan brother devoted to the Blessed Sacrament.
misc: “Communion is a reward for the good.”
lessons.mem: “My flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink.” (John 6:55)
lessons.hook: Read John 6:51–60. Ask: “Why did many disciples leave? What did Jesus do?” He did not take back his words.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the Real Presence using Scripture and Church teaching.

script.open: Ask, “If someone said, ‘The Eucharist is just a symbol,’ how would you respond, using only the Bible?” Let students try. “The earliest Christians had to answer this too.”
teach: Say: “The Eucharist is ‘the source and summit of the Christian life.’ The Catechism describes the Eucharist under several names: Lord’s Supper, breaking of bread, Eucharistic assembly, memorial, holy sacrifice, Holy Communion, Holy Mass. It was instituted at the Last Supper (Matthew 26:26-28; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26). It has three aspects. Sacrifice and memorial: the Eucharist re-presents Christ’s sacrifice on the cross. ‘Do this in remembrance of me’ is anamnesis, which makes present. Hebrews 9-10 teaches that Christ’s sacrifice is once for all, and the Mass is not a new one. Real Presence: John 6:51-58 and the words of institution. Communion: union with Christ and each other.”

Say: “The Real Presence. The Church teaches that the whole Christ is present: body, blood, soul and divinity, in each species, under the appearances of bread and wine. The term ‘transubstantiation’ was used to explain how: the substance (what a thing is) changes, while the accidents (appearances) remain. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) used it; Trent confirmed. The Church’s evidence: John 6 (Jesus didn’t retract when many left); 1 Corinthians 10:16 and 11:27-29 (guilty of the body and blood); the unanimous witness of the Fathers (Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Cyril of Jerusalem). Eucharistic miracles, like Lanciano, are signs but not proof.”

Say: “The Eucharist builds the Church, and she is its fruit. The Church teaches that Communion is for those in communion with the Church and in the state of grace. Reverent reception is in the hand or on the tongue, standing or kneeling, with a bow before receiving. The fast is one hour. In the Eucharist we are united to Christ, receive grace to avoid sin, are forgiven venial sins, deepen our unity with the Church and are committed to the poor. Matthew 25 and Mass go together: ‘You cannot claim to honor the Body of Christ in the Eucharist while neglecting his body in the poor,’ as Chrysostom said. Adoration extends the Mass. Every Mass ends by sending us out.”
ask: Name three aspects of the Eucharist. (Sacrifice and memorial, real presence, communion.)
What is transubstantiation? (The substance changes; appearances remain.)
How does the Eucharist relate to the poor? (We cannot honor Christ’s body at the altar and ignore it in the poor.)
practice: Make a three-column chart: Sacrifice, Presence, Communion, with a Scripture text and a Church teaching for each.
Write the strongest Biblical argument for the Real Presence.
Write a thanksgiving prayer for after Communion (4-5 sentences).
Share one phrase with a partner.
script.close: Pray the Adoro Te Devote (one verse) or “Jesus, I adore you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Spend five minutes in silent thanksgiving after Communion.”

tryit: Outline the three dimensions of the Eucharist.
Pair each with a Scripture text.
Write your own thanksgiving after Communion.
lessons.saintStory:
Paschal Baylon was born in 1540 in Aragon, Spain, to poor farming parents. He worked as a shepherd from age seven. While tending sheep, he would pray and kneel facing the nearest church, when he heard the bell for Mass. He taught himself to read, so he could say prayers from a book, by asking passersby to teach him letters.
At twenty-four he joined the Franciscan Alcantarines as a lay brother. He was assigned to work as porter, cook and gardener, and served as a messenger, traveling on foot across France, which was then a dangerous journey for a Spanish friar, since the Huguenots persecuted Catholics. Once he was stoned for defending the Real Presence in a debate. He spent long hours before the Blessed Sacrament.
He died in 1592 on Pentecost Sunday, as Mass was being celebrated, at the moment of the elevation. In 1897, Pope Leo XIII named him patron of Eucharistic Congresses and societies.

lessons.title: Sin and mercy
lessons.idea: Sin wounds our relationship with God, ourselves and others; mercy heals. Psalm 51 is the model of repentance: “Have mercy on me, O God… create in me a clean heart.” The Church distinguishes mortal and venial sin and always offers forgiveness.
lessons.question: What is sin?
lessons.activity: “Study Psalm 51” (35 min). Students annotate Psalm 51 in sections: confession (1–6), plea for cleansing (7–12), promise to witness (13–17). Note the context (2 Samuel 12). Write a personal version of the psalm for today.
teach: Sin is “an offense against reason, truth and right conscience” and against God (CCC 1849–1851). Mortal sin requires grave matter, full knowledge and deliberate consent (CCC 1857); venial sin weakens charity (CCC 1862–1863).
The root of sin is in the heart (CCC 1853–1854). Capital sins are vices that give rise to others (CCC 1866).
God’s mercy is greater: Jesus forgives sinners (Luke 15). “Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20; CCC 1847).
Address scrupulosity with care; the remedy is trust and spiritual direction.
quiz: Mortal sin requires…|Any wrong act|Public scandal|Grave matter, full knowledge and deliberate consent|Strong feelings|2|CCC 1857.
Psalm 51 teaches that repentance includes…|Waiting|Excusing it|Naming sin honestly, asking for a clean heart and trusting God’s mercy|Hiding the sin|2|Psalm 51:1–12.
Venial sin…|Wounds but does not destroy friendship with God (CCC 1863)|Is unimportant|Breaks charity completely|Cannot be forgiven|0|CCC 1862–1863.
lessons.life: Pray Psalm 51 slowly.
lessons.saint: Moses the Black: a former robber who became a desert monk and a teacher of mercy.
lessons.mem: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.” (Psalm 51:10)
lessons.hook: Read Psalm 51:1–4. Ask: “What does David admit? What does he ask?” He doesn’t excuse himself; he appeals to mercy.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the effects of sin and the shape of repentance in Psalm 51.

script.open: Ask, “What is the difference between making a mistake, doing wrong, and sinning? Are they the same?” Take answers. “The Church has a careful vocabulary.”
teach: Say: “Sin is ‘an offense against reason, truth and right conscience; it is a failure in genuine love for God and neighbor’ (CCC 1849). The tradition has always seen that sin is first an offense against God (Psalm 51:4: ‘Against you, you only, have I sinned’), and also wounds our nature and the community. Origin: original sin and personal sin. Distinctions: mortal sin destroys charity and requires conversion, usually through Confession; venial sin weakens charity but doesn’t destroy it. Three conditions for mortal sin: grave matter, full knowledge, deliberate consent. Grave matter is specified by the Ten Commandments. Culpability can be lessened by ignorance, fear, habit or force.”

Say: “Sins can be classified by their object (what is done), by the virtues they oppose, by commandments, by whether they are of thought, word, deed or omission. The seven capital sins are root vices. Sin has consequences: loss of charity, deprivation of grace, eternal punishment if unrepented, temporal punishment, and the formation of vices. Social sin: structures of sin that arise from personal sins. Sin spreads: we can cooperate in the sins of others by commanding, advising, praising or defending them. Pope John Paul II said the loss of the sense of sin is a mark of our age. Sin is real; the alternative would make forgiveness meaningless.”

Say: “The answer to sin is mercy. Luke 15 gathers three parables: lost sheep, lost coin, lost son. God seeks the sinner. ‘There will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.’ Mercy doesn’t deny sin; it forgives it. The prodigal returns and the father runs. The Catechism says: ‘There is no offense, however serious, that the Church cannot forgive.’ (CCC 982) Conversion is more than feeling bad: it is metanoia, a change of mind and heart. Pope Francis in Misericordiae Vultus calls God’s name mercy. Moses the Black, Augustine, Mary Magdalene and Peter show that mercy makes saints out of sinners.”
ask: What is sin? (An offense against reason, truth and right conscience; a failure of love.)
What three conditions make a sin mortal? (Grave matter, full knowledge, deliberate consent.)
Is any sin unforgivable by the Church? (No; the Church can forgive any sin.)
practice: Prepare scenarios with varying details (grave matter but unknowing; deliberate but small matter; compelled by fear).
Decide for each: mortal, venial or not culpable? Which condition is missing?
Write what repentance requires in each case.
Pray Psalm 51 together.
script.close: Pray the Act of Contrition. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read the parable of the prodigal son.”

tryit: Distinguish kinds of sin.
Use the three conditions for mortal sin.
Write what repentance requires.
lessons.saintStory:
Moses was an Ethiopian slave in the fourth century who was dismissed by his master for stealing and violence. He became the leader of a gang of robbers in Egypt, a huge, fearsome man. According to the desert fathers, one day he was fleeing the authorities, and hid in the monastery in Scete. The monks’ way of life moved him. He stayed, repented and became a monk.
He struggled for years with temptations and with his past. He went to Abba Isidore, who took him out to the roof at dawn and showed him the sun rising: “Slowly, slowly, the light comes.” Over time, he became a wise elder. When a brother was judged for a fault, Moses came to the council carrying a leaking basket of sand. When asked, he said, “My sins are running out behind me and I do not see them, and today I am coming to judge the sins of another.” The brothers forgave the offender.
Moses was killed by raiders around 405. He is the patron of nonviolence in the Church.

lessons.title: Confession
lessons.idea: In the Sacrament of Penance, a penitent confesses sins to a priest, who gives absolution in Christ’s name. The sacrament requires contrition, confession, satisfaction and absolution. The seal of confession is inviolable. Frequent Confession deepens conversion.
lessons.question: Why confess to a priest?
lessons.activity: “Respond to an objection” (40 min). Students prepare responses to: “Why confess to a priest, not directly to God?”, “Who is the priest to forgive?”, “Isn’t it embarrassing?” Use John 20:23, 2 Corinthians 5:18–20 and James 5:16. Practice a respectful dialogue.
teach: The sacrament goes by many names: Penance, Reconciliation, Confession, Conversion (CCC 1423–1424). Acts of the penitent: contrition, confession, satisfaction (CCC 1450–1460).
The priest acts in persona Christi (CCC 1461–1467). He is bound by the sacramental seal, absolutely and without exception (CCC 1467).
Mortal sins must be confessed in kind and number; the faithful are obliged to confess at least once a year (CCC 1456–1457, 2042). Frequent Confession is recommended (CCC 1458).
Effects: reconciliation with God and the Church, remission of eternal punishment, peace of conscience (CCC 1468–1470).
quiz: Which are the acts of the penitent?|Contrition, confession and satisfaction (CCC 1450)|Absolution and penance only|Silence|Gifts|0|CCC 1450.

Perfect contrition differs from imperfect contrition in that perfect contrition…|Comes from fear|Needs no confession|Replaces absolution|Comes from love of God|3|CCC 1452–1453; it still requires a firm resolve to confess.
The seal of confession forbids the priest to…|Absolve|Reveal anything heard in confession, under any circumstance (CCC 1467)|Hear women|Give penance|1|CCC 1467.
lessons.life: Make a good Confession and write a thank-you prayer.
lessons.saint: Leopold Mandić: a tiny Capuchin who heard confessions for thirty years in a Padua cell.
misc: “I can just confess privately to God.”
lessons.mem: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, and will forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)
lessons.hook: Read John 20:21–23. Ask: “Why would Jesus breathe on the apostles and give them this power?” Ask students to compare to Jesus forgiving sins in Mark 2.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe the four parts of the sacrament and answer one objection.

script.open: Ask, “What makes it hard to say sorry out loud? Why does speaking it matter? Is it enough to just be sorry privately?” Take answers.
teach: Read John 20:19-23. Say: “On Easter night Jesus appeared to the apostles and said, ‘Peace be with you… Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.’ This is the institution of the sacrament of Reconciliation (also called Penance or Confession). Notice that he gave the power to men, not just directly to God. The priest acts in persona Christi. Why a priest? Because sin is also against the Church; because we need to say it aloud; because we need to hear the words of absolution.”

Say: “The acts of the penitent are contrition, confession and satisfaction. Contrition: sorrow of the soul and detestation of sin with the resolution not to sin again. Perfect contrition, from love of God, forgives venial sins immediately and mortal sins with the intention to confess. Imperfect contrition (attrition), from fear or the ugliness of sin, is enough for the sacrament. Confession: all mortal sins (in kind and number) must be confessed. Venial sins are good to confess. Satisfaction: the penance given by the priest to repair the harm and heal. The priest’s act is absolution: ‘God, the Father of mercies, through the death and resurrection of his Son has reconciled the world to himself and sent the Holy Spirit among us for the forgiveness of sins; through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.’”

Say: “Rite. Greeting; Sign of the Cross; reading of the Word (optional); confession of sins; the priest gives counsel and a penance; act of contrition; absolution; thanksgiving; dismissal. Face-to-face or behind a screen. Seal of confession: absolute; the priest can never reveal what he hears, even under threat of death. Effects: reconciliation with God and the Church, peace of conscience, spiritual consolation, forgiveness of eternal punishment for mortal sins, and a remission of temporal punishment. The Church requires confessing grave sins at least once a year, and before Communion if in mortal sin. Frequent confession is encouraged. Three forms of rite: individual, communal with individual confession, and general absolution (only in grave necessity). A good examination of conscience uses the Ten Commandments or the Beatitudes.”
ask: What are the acts of the penitent? (Contrition, confession, satisfaction.)
What does the priest do? (Gives counsel and penance, absolves in the person of Christ.)
What is the seal of confession? (The priest may never reveal what he hears.)
practice: Make a flowchart of the rite with who speaks at each step.
Write an examination of conscience for your age based on the Ten Commandments (7-10 questions).
Memorize the words of the Act of Contrition.
Plan when you will go to Confession next.
script.close: Pray the Act of Contrition aloud together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Schedule a Confession this month.”

tryit: Walk through the rite of Reconciliation.
Mark what the penitent does and what the priest does.
Prepare an examination of conscience.
lessons.saintStory:
Bogdan Mandić was born in 1866 in Herceg Novi, in present-day Montenegro. He was a tiny man, barely four feet five inches, with a speech impediment and weak health. He joined the Capuchins, taking the name Leopold, and was ordained in 1890. He dreamed of going to the East to work for the reunion of Orthodox and Catholics, but his superiors judged his health unfit, and he spent his life in Italy.
He was assigned to Padua, where he spent most of his priestly life in a small cell by the church, hearing confessions, for ten to fifteen hours a day. People of all kinds came, including priests and academics. He was gentle and patient, and many left in tears. When asked why he was so merciful, he said, “I give the people all the forgiveness that Jesus gave. If the Lord reproaches me for being too generous, I will say, ‘It was you who gave me such a bad example.’”
He died in 1942, and was canonized in 1983.

lessons.title: Anointing of the Sick
lessons.idea: In the Anointing of the Sick, the priest anoints with oil and prays for strength, forgiveness and comfort in serious illness or old age. It prepares the soul for healing or for passing to the Father. It may be repeated.
lessons.question: Who may receive it?
lessons.activity: “Interview a chaplain” (40 min). Invite a hospital or hospice chaplain, or watch an interview. Prepare questions: What do you see in suffering? How do you minister to the dying? What do families need? Write a reflection on how to accompany the sick.
teach: The sacrament is for those seriously ill or weakened by age (CCC 1514–1515). Its effects: uniting the sick person with the Passion, strength, peace, forgiveness, and sometimes physical healing (CCC 1520–1523).
The minister is a priest. The matter is oil blessed by the bishop (or by the priest in need), and the form is the prayer (CCC 1519, 1512–1513).
Viaticum, Communion for the dying, is the “food for the journey” (CCC 1524–1525). Together with Penance and Anointing, these are the last sacraments.
It is not “last rites” only. Encourage receiving it before surgery or in serious illness.
talk: How do we accompany the sick?
quiz: The Anointing of the Sick is for…|Only priests|Those seriously ill or weakened by age (CCC 1514)|Only the dying|Only the baptized who ask in writing|1|CCC 1514–1515.
Viaticum is…|A prayer|Communion given to the dying as food for the journey (CCC 1524)|A funeral|Anointing oil|1|CCC 1524.
Which effect belongs to the Anointing of the Sick?|Priesthood|Removal of death|Strength, peace and courage, forgiveness of sins and sometimes physical healing (CCC 1520)|Guaranteed cure|2|CCC 1520.
lessons.life: Visit a hospital or nursing home.
lessons.saint: John of God: a bookseller who turned a rented house into a hospital for the poor.
misc: “Last rites are only for the dying.”
lessons.mem: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.” (James 5:14)
lessons.hook: Read James 5:14–15. Ask: “What do the elders do? What is promised?” Notice anointing, prayer, faith, forgiveness and healing.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain who may receive the sacrament, its effects and how to support the sick.

script.open: Ask, “What do people need when they are seriously ill: not just medicine, but what else? Who has been with someone who was ill? What helped?” Take answers.
teach: Read James 5:14-15. Say: “‘Is any among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick man, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.’ The sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick has its roots in Jesus’ healing ministry (Mark 6:13) and the apostles’ practice. The Council of Trent taught that this is a sacrament instituted by Christ. For centuries it was called ‘Extreme Unction’ and was given only to the dying; Vatican II restored the fuller understanding as for the seriously ill and elderly.”

Say: “Who may receive it: any baptized Catholic who has reached the age of reason and is in danger from illness or old age. This includes before serious surgery, and those weakened by old age. It may be repeated if the illness worsens or recurs. The minister is a priest or bishop. The rite: laying on of hands in silence, then anointing the forehead and hands with the oil of the sick (blessed by the bishop at the Chrism Mass) with the words, ‘Through this holy anointing may the Lord in his love and mercy help you with the grace of the Holy Spirit. May the Lord who frees you from sin save you and raise you up.’ If possible, it is celebrated within Mass, with the community. For one near death, it is combined with Penance and Viaticum.”

Say: “Effects: a gift of the Holy Spirit, strengthening, peace and courage against the difficulties of illness; union with the Passion of Christ for the good of oneself and the Church; forgiveness of sins if the sick person was unable to confess; restoration of health, if it is conducive to salvation; preparation for the passage to eternal life. Sickness isn’t a punishment for sin (John 9:3); it’s an occasion for grace. The Church’s care for the sick continues Jesus’ ministry: hospitals began as Christian foundations. Visiting the sick is a work of mercy. The sacrament is often feared as ‘last rites’; it’s better to call the priest early. We should also support the caregivers. Viaticum, Communion for the dying, is ‘food for the journey.’”
ask: Who may receive the Anointing? (Baptized Catholics seriously ill or weakened by age.)
What does the sacrament do? (Strengthens, forgives sins, unites with Christ’s suffering, may heal.)
What is Viaticum? (Communion for the dying.)
practice: Match each sign (oil, laying on of hands, prayer of faith) with its effect and Bible text.
Write a short explanation of the sacrament for a worried grandparent.
Plan a visit, call or card to someone ill.
Write a prayer for the sick.
script.close: Pray for the sick of your parish by name. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Visit or call someone who is ill.”

tryit: Describe the Anointing in your own words.
Pair each sign with an effect.
Write a plan to visit someone who is ill.
lessons.saintStory:
João Cidade was born in 1495 in Portugal, and as a young man was a soldier and shepherd. Around the age of forty, in Granada, Spain, he heard a sermon by John of Avila, and was so moved by his own sins that he cried out and beat himself publicly. People thought he was mad, and he was committed to an asylum, where he was treated harshly. The cruel treatment of patients stirred in him a determination to help the sick. John of Avila visited him and told him to take action.
He was released and opened a bookshop. In 1539 he rented a house in Granada and filled it with poor, sick people, begging for food and medicine for them. He did the work with his own hands. When the Royal Hospital caught fire in 1549, he is said to have carried patients out through the flames.
He died in 1550 on his knees, at fifty-five. The followers who gathered around him became the Brothers Hospitallers of St. John of God. He is the patron of hospitals, nurses and the sick.

lessons.title: Holy Orders
lessons.idea: Holy Orders confers sacred power to teach, sanctify and govern in Christ’s name. It has three degrees: bishop, priest, deacon. The ministerial priesthood differs in essence from the common priesthood of the faithful. The Church ordains only baptized men, following Christ’s choice of the Twelve.
lessons.question: Why only men?
lessons.activity: “Study CCC 1577 and Ordinatio Sacerdotalis” (40 min). Students read CCC 1577 and John Paul II’s Ordinatio Sacerdotalis (1994): the arguments (Christ’s choice, apostolic practice, Church’s constant Tradition) and what it does not say (women’s dignity). Debate respectfully, with guidelines.
teach: Holy Orders is the sacrament through which the mission entrusted by Christ to his apostles continues until the end of time (CCC 1536). The three degrees: episcopate, presbyterate, diaconate (CCC 1554).
The priest acts in persona Christi capitis (CCC 1548). Ordination imprints an indelible character (CCC 1582).
“Only a baptized man (vir) validly receives sacred ordination” (CCC 1577). Jesus freely chose men for the Twelve; the Church has no authority to change this (CCC 1577–1578; John Paul II).
Affirm women’s dignity and roles in the Church (CCC 2334–2336). Distinguish equal dignity from identical function.
quiz: The Church ordains only baptized men because…|Women are inferior|Christ chose men as apostles and the Church has no authority to change it (CCC 1577; Ordinatio Sacerdotalis)|Men are holier|It is cultural|1|CCC 1577–1578.
The priest acts “in persona Christi capitis,” which means he…|Is sinless|Replaces Christ|Acts in the person of Christ the head of the Church (CCC 1548)|Is above others|2|CCC 1548.
The three degrees of Orders are…|Monk, priest, deacon|Pope, cardinal, bishop|Priest, deacon, acolyte|Bishop, priest, deacon|3|CCC 1554.
lessons.life: Pray for your priests.
lessons.saint: Karl Leisner: a seminarian ordained secretly in Dachau and dying of tuberculosis soon after.
misc: “The exclusion of women is only cultural.”
lessons.mem: “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.” (Hebrews 5:6)
lessons.hook: Read Hebrews 5:1–10. Ask: “What does the high priest do? How is Christ the perfect High Priest?” The priesthood participates in his.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the three degrees of Orders and the Church’s reasons for ordaining only men.

script.open: Ask, “If the Church were short of priests, could we simply choose a faithful layman to celebrate Mass? What would be missing?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Holy Orders is ‘the sacrament through which the mission entrusted by Christ to his apostles continues to be exercised in the Church until the end of time.’ (CCC 1536) It has three degrees: episcopate, presbyterate, diaconate. The bishop is the fullness of the priesthood; he teaches, sanctifies and governs. Priests are co-workers of the bishop; they preach, celebrate the Eucharist and other sacraments, and lead parishes. Deacons are ordained ‘not unto priesthood but unto ministry’: they proclaim the Gospel, preach, assist at Mass, baptize, witness marriages, and serve in charity. Only bishops can ordain.”

Say: “The rite. The essential rite is the laying on of hands by the bishop and the consecratory prayer asking God for the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. For a priest, the ordinand is presented, elected, examined, promises obedience; the Litany of the Saints is sung while he lies prostrate; the bishop lays on hands in silence; then the prayer of ordination. Explanatory rites: anointing of the hands with chrism, giving the paten and chalice, the vestments (stole and chasuble). Effects: a special configuration to Christ as Priest, Teacher and Shepherd, and a permanent character; one cannot be ‘un-ordained,’ though one may be dispensed from obligations.”

Say: “Who may be ordained: baptized men called by God and the Church. The Church holds that she has no authority to ordain women (John Paul II, Ordinatio Sacerdotalis). In the Latin Church, priests are normally celibate; Eastern Catholic priests may be married. Candidates go through years of formation in a seminary: human, spiritual, intellectual and pastoral. A vocation is a call from God, confirmed by the Church. The priest acts in persona Christi capitis. Though the priest is an ordinary man with weaknesses, the sacraments are valid regardless. Pope Benedict XVI said that the priesthood is ‘the love of the heart of Jesus.’ We pray for vocations: ‘Ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.’ (Matthew 9:38) We also support our priests: with prayer, friendship, and respect.”
ask: What are the three degrees of Holy Orders? (Bishop, priest, deacon.)
What is the essential rite? (Laying on of hands and the prayer of consecration by the bishop.)
Why can’t ordination be undone? (It confers an indelible character.)
practice: Make a table: Bishop, Priest, Deacon with columns for role, faculties, and Scripture roots.
Write a letter of thanks to a priest or deacon, mentioning something specific.
Compose a prayer for vocations.
Pray it daily this week.
script.close: Pray: “Lord of the harvest, send laborers.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray daily for vocations.”

tryit: Describe the three degrees of Holy Orders.
Mark what is unique to each.
Write a prayer for vocations.
lessons.saintStory:
Karl Leisner was born in 1915 in Germany. As a young man he was active in Catholic youth groups, which Hitler’s regime tried to eliminate. He kept a diary. In 1939 he was ordained a deacon, but was soon arrested, after overhearing that he had said something critical of an assassination attempt on Hitler. He was sent to Dachau concentration camp, where he contracted tuberculosis.
By 1944, he was dying. A French bishop, Gabriel Piguet, was also a prisoner at Dachau. Plans were made to smuggle in what was needed. On December 17, 1944, in the camp chapel, Bishop Piguet ordained Karl Leisner a priest, with a few trusted prisoners present. A fellow prisoner made the vestments secretly, and the ordination oil and the ring were smuggled in. A few days later, on December 26, Karl celebrated his first and only Mass.
Karl was freed in 1945 when the camp was liberated, but died of tuberculosis in August. He was twenty-nine. He was beatified in 1996. He shows what the priesthood means: a call to offer Mass at any cost.

lessons.title: Marriage as a sacrament
lessons.idea: Marriage is a covenant of love between a baptized man and woman, established by God and raised by Christ to a sacrament. Its properties are unity and indissolubility; its ends are the good of the spouses and the procreation and education of children. Consent makes the marriage.
lessons.question: Why is marriage indissoluble?
lessons.activity: “Debate” (40 min). Teams debate a proposition such as “Marriage should be seen as a permanent covenant, not a contract renewable at will.” They use Scripture (Genesis 2:24; Mark 10:6–9), natural law and experience. Conclude with each student writing how a covenant differs from a contract.
teach: Marriage is “a covenant by which a man and a woman establish between themselves a partnership of the whole of life” (CCC 1601; Canon 1055). The consent of the spouses makes it (CCC 1626–1628).
The goods of marriage: unity, indissolubility, fidelity, openness to children (CCC 1643–1654). A valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved (CCC 1640).
Impediments and annulment: the Church can declare that a union was never valid (CCC 1629–1637; see the lesson on annulment).
The spouses are the ministers; the Church’s witness is essential. Marriage preparation matters.
quiz: In the Latin Church the ministers of Matrimony are…|The bride and groom, with the priest or deacon as official witness (CCC 1623)|The parents|The priest|The state|0|CCC 1623.

An annulment declares that…|The marriage is dissolved|The children are illegitimate|The couple are divorced|A putative marriage was never valid because of a defect in consent, form or capacity (CCC 1629)|3|CCC 1629; legitimacy is not affected.
Which is a good of marriage named in the Catechism?|Equality of income|Convenience|Unity, fidelity, indissolubility and openness to children (CCC 1643–1654)|Wealth|2|CCC 1643–1654.
lessons.life: Read the Rite of Marriage.
lessons.saint: Luigi and Maria Beltrame Quattrocchi: a married couple beatified together who opened their home in wartime.
lessons.mem: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.” (Genesis 2:24)
lessons.hook: Read Ephesians 5:25–32 and Genesis 2:24. Ask: “What does it mean that marriage reflects Christ and the Church?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to state the goods of marriage and explain why consent is essential.

script.open: Ask, “What are the promises made at a wedding? Why are they made in front of others?” Take answers. “Today we look at what marriage is, in Catholic teaching.”
teach: Read Genesis 2:24 and Matthew 19:4-6. Say: “‘Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said, “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one”? So they are no longer two but one. What therefore God has joined together, let not man put asunder.’ The Church teaches that marriage is a covenant by which a man and a woman establish between themselves a partnership of the whole of life, ordered by its nature to the good of the spouses and to the procreation and education of offspring. Between baptized persons, it has been raised by Christ to the dignity of a sacrament.”

Say: “The essential properties: unity (one man and one woman) and indissolubility (permanent until death). The ends: the good of the spouses (unitive) and the procreation and education of children. The consent is what makes the marriage: ‘an act of the will by which a man and a woman mutually give and accept each other.’ (CCC 1625) It must be free, full, faithful, and fruitful. The spouses themselves are the ministers of the sacrament in the Latin Church; the priest or deacon is the official witness. A Catholic marriage should be in the Church, with the proper canonical form. The rite: the entrance, liturgy of the Word, the questions about freedom, fidelity and openness to children, the exchange of vows, the blessing and exchange of rings, the nuptial blessing, and usually a Mass.”

Say: “The grace of the sacrament perfects the couple’s love, strengthens their indissoluble unity, and helps them to holiness. Paul calls marriage a great mystery that signifies Christ’s love for the Church (Ephesians 5:25-32). The couple become a sign of that love. Preparation: engaged couples undergo pastoral preparation, often a course of six months, including natural family planning, communication and finances. Impediments: age, impotence, a prior bond, disparity of cult (marrying an unbaptized person requires a dispensation), blood relationship, and others. The Church also recognizes marriages between non-Catholics and the Pauline privilege. Marriage is a vocation. Conditions for a good marriage: faith, communication, forgiveness, generosity, prayer. The family is the ‘domestic church.’”
ask: What are the properties of marriage? (Unity and indissolubility.)
What makes a marriage? (The free consent of the spouses.)
Who are the ministers in the Latin Church? (The spouses themselves.)
practice: Create a checklist for valid Catholic marriage: baptized or dispensation, free consent, proper form, no impediments, openness to children and permanence.
Write the vows you would want to make in your own words.
Write a prayer for your future spouse or vocation.
Share in pairs.
script.close: Pray for married couples and engaged couples. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask a married couple about their wedding vows.”

tryit: Outline the properties and ends of marriage.
Check what makes a marriage valid.
Draft a prayer for your future marriage.
lessons.saintStory:
Luigi Beltrame Quattrocchi (1880–1951) was a lawyer, and Maria Corsini (1884–1965) was a teacher and writer, in Rome. They married in 1905 and had four children. One pregnancy was complicated; doctors advised that the baby could not be saved and Maria’s life was in danger. They trusted God, and their daughter Enrichetta was born healthy.
The couple lived their faith in daily life. They prayed the Rosary and went to Mass together, and their home was open to friends, relatives and the needy. Three of their children entered religious life: two became priests, and one a Trappist nun. During World War II, the family hid Jews and other refugees in their home. Maria also worked with the Red Cross, was involved in Catholic Action, and helped to found a school.
They were beatified together in 2001, the first married couple in history to be beatified as a couple. Pope John Paul II said that they lived “ordinary life in an extraordinary way.”

lessons.title: Family and vocation
lessons.idea: The Christian family is the domestic church: a school of faith, prayer and love where children first learn about God. Parents are the first teachers. The Holy Family, especially Joseph’s fidelity and Mary’s trust, is the model.
lessons.question: What makes a home holy?
lessons.activity: “Plan a family prayer” (35 min). Students plan a simple family prayer pattern (meal blessing, bedtime blessing, Sunday Mass, seasonal customs like the Advent wreath) that suits their home. They write a short script. They also design an act of service for their family.
teach: The family is “the domestic church” (CCC 1655–1658; Lumen Gentium 11). Parents are the first heralds of the faith (CCC 2223–2226).
The family is the original cell of social life (CCC 2207). Duties: children honor parents (CCC 2214–2220); parents educate and respect their children (CCC 2221–2231).
Families come in many shapes; the Church cares for single parents, blended families and those in difficulty. Pope Francis’ Amoris Laetitia accompanies families with mercy.
Prayer and practice at home matter more than lessons.
talk: What is the role of parents?
quiz: Calling the family a “domestic church” means…|The home is the first place where faith is taught, prayed and lived (CCC 1655–1658)|Parents are priests|A home must be a chapel|Church is optional|0|CCC 1655–1658.
Parents’ primary duty in education is…|To be the first teachers of their children in faith and virtue (CCC 2223)|To delegate|To leave faith to schools|To avoid correction|0|CCC 2223.
Amoris Laetitia asks the Church to…|Close parishes|Accompany all families, with mercy and truth|Abolish doctrine|Ignore broken families|1|Pope Francis, 2016.
lessons.life: Establish a family prayer time.
lessons.saint: Louis IX of France: a king, husband and father of eleven who also served lepers at his table.
misc: “Only perfect families can be a domestic church.”
lessons.mem: “As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.” (Joshua 24:15)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 2:41–52. Ask: “What does this family do together? What does it suffer?” A real family with real worry.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe three habits of a domestic church and commit to one.

script.open: Ask, “What did your family do that taught you something about faith, even without words? A meal, a habit, a way of treating people?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The Council called the family the ‘domestic church’ (LG 11). The Catechism: ‘The Christian home is the place where children receive the first proclamation of the faith.’ (CCC 1656) Family life is a school of virtue and faith. Parents are the first teachers of their children. They pass on faith by prayer together, by the sacraments, by example, by hospitality, by forgiving one another. Gaudium et Spes calls the family a ‘school of deeper humanity.’ John Paul II in Familiaris Consortio 17 spoke of the four tasks of the family: forming a community of persons, serving life, participating in society, and sharing in the Church’s life and mission.”

Say: “Vocation: every person has a vocation; the word means ‘call.’ The first call is to holiness. The four states of life: marriage, ordained ministry, consecrated life (religious life, consecrated virgins, hermits), and the single life dedicated to God and others. Single people are not people without vocation. Some are single by circumstance; some by choice for service; some are ‘single for the Kingdom’ as lay missionaries. We discern vocation through prayer, the sacraments, honesty about gifts, advice from wise people, and the desires of the heart purified by God. God calls at times in surprising ways. Decisions about vocation should be made freely; no one should be pressured.”

Say: “Trials. Families struggle with illness, financial stress, conflict, divorce, addiction and loss. The Church supports them. The sacraments strengthen. Forgiveness at home matters. Pope Francis in Amoris Laetitia (2016) says that love in the family is ‘patient, kind, not jealous,’ drawing on 1 Corinthians 13. Practices that help: a family meal with grace; Sunday Mass together; a family Rosary or night prayer; Advent wreath and Lenten traditions; blessing children; service together; talking about faith. Even if your family doesn’t practice, you can make your life a witness. You are also forming your future family now by the habits you build.”
ask: What is the domestic church? (The family as the first place of faith.)
What are the four states of life? (Marriage, ordained ministry, consecrated life, dedicated single life.)
What practices build a family’s faith? (Prayer, Sunday Mass, forgiveness, service, meals.)
practice: List five practices of a family that is a ‘domestic church.’
Rate how many are in your home now, without judgment.
Choose one small practice to begin this week.
Write a prayer for your family.
script.close: Pray the Prayer for the Family or “Holy Family, pray for us.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Start one family practice this week.”

tryit: Describe the domestic church.
List what makes a home a school of faith.
Choose a family practice to start.
lessons.saintStory:
Louis IX was born in 1214 and became king of France at twelve, with his mother Blanche of Castile as regent. She taught him that she would rather see him dead than commit a mortal sin. He married Margaret of Provence in 1234 and they had eleven children. He was devoted to his wife and children, and took care of their religious education.
He was a just king. He is said to have sat under an oak at Vincennes, hearing the petitions of any who came. He established a system of appeals, forbade trial by combat, and cared for the poor. Each day he heard Mass, prayed the Hours, and fed the poor at his table, sometimes serving lepers with his own hands. He built the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris to house the crown of thorns.
He went on two crusades, was captured on the first, and died of disease on the second, in Tunis in 1270. He is the patron of tertiaries and French kings. He showed how a lay person in public life can pursue holiness in marriage, family and office.

lessons.title: The dignity of the person and the Beatitudes
lessons.idea: Every person is made in God’s image and called to beatitude: to share in God’s own happiness. The Beatitudes name the attitudes and actions that lead there, and they answer the natural desire for happiness.
lessons.question: Where is happiness found?
lessons.activity: “Reflect” (30 min). Students choose one Beatitude and write on the cost, the promise and a person they know who lives it. They list one decision this week that expresses it. Class shares anonymously.
teach: Human dignity: created in the image of God, with intellect and will (CCC 1700–1709). Our vocation is beatitude (CCC 1718–1719).
The Beatitudes depict Christ’s own character and the actions of the disciple (CCC 1716–1717). They reorient our desires toward God (CCC 1723–1729).
Happiness is found only in God (CCC 1718, 1723). Thomas Aquinas: happiness is the vision of God.
The moral life starts with who we are and what we are for, not with a list of prohibitions.
quiz: The Beatitudes describe…|Judges|The attitudes and path of the disciple and the happiness God offers (CCC 1716–1717)|Church rules|An easy life|1|CCC 1716–1717.
Human dignity, in Catholic teaching, comes from…|Achievement|Being made in God’s image with intellect and will (CCC 1700–1702)|Social status|Law|1|CCC 1700–1702.
According to Aquinas and the Catechism, real happiness is found…|In power|Only in God (CCC 1718, 1723)|In wealth|In pleasure|1|CCC 1718.
lessons.life: Rewrite the Beatitudes for today.
lessons.saint: Jerzy Popiełuszko: a young Polish priest killed for preaching “overcome evil with good.”
misc: “Morality is just a list of don’ts.”
lessons.mem: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” (Matthew 5:8)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do you think is the secret to being happy?” List answers. Read Matthew 5:1–12.
lessons.assess: Ask students to link human dignity to the Beatitudes in a short paragraph.

script.open: Write on the board: “Why can’t I do whatever I want with another person?” Ask for the strongest reasons students can give, from any worldview. Then say, “The Church’s answer is a claim about what a human being is.”
teach: Say: “The foundation of Catholic morality is human dignity. Genesis 1:27: ‘God created man in his own image.’ Each person is made in God’s image, has an intellect and free will, is capable of knowing and loving, and is called to communion with God. The Catechism: ‘The dignity of the human person is rooted in his creation in the image and likeness of God.’ (CCC 1700) It was elevated by the Incarnation: the Son took human nature. It is not earned by usefulness or taken away by weakness or sin. Human beings have rights because they have dignity, and duties because they are persons.”
