Say: “Our end is beatitude, happiness with God. The Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3-12) are the Church’s picture of the happy life. Each beatitude names a blessing and a promise. They are the heart of Jesus’ preaching and a portrait of his own life, and of the path of the saints. The Catechism says the Beatitudes ‘respond to the natural desire for happiness’ (CCC 1718) and ‘depict the countenance of Jesus Christ and portray his charity.’ They show the way: poverty of spirit, meekness, purity of heart, mercy, hunger for justice, peacemaking, perseverance under persecution. They invert the world’s ideas of success: they aren’t rules to follow to earn heaven, but a way of seeing and living under the Kingdom.”

Say: “Implications. If every person has dignity, then life must be protected from conception to natural death; the poor and weak deserve special care; slavery, torture, human trafficking and racism are evils; so are using people as means. Dignity also means we have responsibilities: to seek the truth, to act freely and responsibly, to love. Popiełuszko lived this: he defended workers’ dignity by non-violent means, and paid with his life. The secret of the Beatitudes: Jesus lives them first. He was poor in spirit, meek, merciful, peacemaker, persecuted. When we live them, we are living in Christ. Pope Francis wrote, ‘The Beatitudes are like a Christian’s identity card.’ (Gaudete et Exsultate 63)”
ask: Where does human dignity come from? (Creation in God’s image, raised by the Incarnation.)
What is our final end? (Beatitude, happiness with God.)
What does Gaudete et Exsultate call the Beatitudes? (A Christian’s identity card.)
practice: Pick three Beatitudes and describe what each looks like at a school or workplace.
List three things that violate human dignity, with one action to resist each.
Write a one-paragraph answer to someone who says dignity depends on ability.
Share one.
script.close: Pray the Beatitudes slowly. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Choose a Beatitude to live this week.”

tryit: Explain why every person has dignity.
Apply the Beatitudes to a modern setting.
List what dignity rules out.
lessons.saintStory:
Jerzy Popiełuszko was born in 1947 in a Polish farming village. He was a sickly boy, an altar server who walked miles to Mass. As a seminarian, he was drafted into the army, where he was harassed for his faith. He was ordained in 1972 and served in Warsaw.
In 1980, when the Solidarity movement was created, he celebrated Mass for striking steelworkers. During martial law in 1981, he began holding monthly “Masses for the Homeland” at St. Stanislaus Kostka Church in Warsaw, drawing tens of thousands. In his homilies, he preached the dignity of work, truth and freedom, and repeated Paul: “Overcome evil with good.” He always urged non-violence.
The communist security service harassed him, interrogated him, and tried to frame him. On October 19, 1984, three secret police officers kidnapped him and beat him to death. He was thirty-seven. A huge crowd of hundreds of thousands attended his funeral. He was beatified in 2010. His grave is one of Poland’s most visited.

lessons.title: Freedom, conscience and natural law
lessons.idea: Freedom is the power to act for the good; conscience is the judgment of reason about right and wrong; natural law is the participation of rational creatures in God’s eternal law. These three are the foundations of moral life.
lessons.question: What is natural law?
lessons.activity: “Discussion” (40 min). Students explore: Is there a moral law all humans can know? Evidence (universal prohibitions on murder, theft), objections (cultural relativism), responses. Compare with the Decalogue. Draw a diagram connecting freedom, conscience and natural law.
teach: Freedom is the power to act or not act (CCC 1731). It grows as we choose the good; sin diminishes it (CCC 1739–1742).
Conscience: “a judgment of reason by which the human person recognizes the moral quality of a concrete act” (CCC 1778). It must be formed and followed (CCC 1783–1790).
Natural law: “nothing other than the light of understanding placed in us by God” (Aquinas; CCC 1954–1960). It is universal and unchangeable, the basis for human rights.
The Old Law and New Law complete natural law (CCC 1961–1974).
talk: How does it relate to conscience?
quiz: Natural law is…|A feeling|A civil statute|The moral law written on the human heart and knowable by reason (CCC 1954–1955)|Only for Catholics|2|CCC 1954–1955.
A person must always follow a certain judgment of conscience, but also…|Never question it|Work to form it well (CCC 1783–1785)|Hide it|Ask no one|1|CCC 1783–1785, 1790.
True freedom, in the Church’s teaching, is…|Escape from law|Absence of authority|Doing anything one wants|The power to choose the good, which grows with virtue (CCC 1731–1733)|3|CCC 1731–1733.
lessons.life: Read about natural law in CCC.
lessons.saint: Rupert Mayer: a Jesuit preacher in Munich who would not stop preaching when the Nazis forbade it.
lessons.mem: “They show that what the law requires is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness.” (Romans 2:15)
lessons.hook: Read Romans 2:14–16. Ask: “How can people who do not know the law still do what it requires?” Introduce natural law.
lessons.assess: Ask students to define freedom, conscience and natural law and show how they connect.

script.open: Ask, “Is a person free if they can do anything they want? Is a fish free if it leaves the water? What does it mean to be truly free?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Freedom is ‘the power, rooted in reason and will, to act or not to act, to do this or that, and so to perform deliberate actions on one’s own responsibility.’ (CCC 1731) It makes us responsible for our acts. The more we do good, the freer we become. Jesus: ‘If you continue in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.’ (John 8:31-32) Freedom is not license, the idea that we can do what we want. Sin enslaves: ‘Everyone who commits sin is a slave to sin.’ (John 8:34) True freedom is freedom for the good. Freedom has limits: facts, others’ rights, the moral law.”

Say: “The moral law is the work of divine Wisdom. Natural law is the moral law ‘written on the heart’ (Romans 2:14-15), accessible to reason, which expresses the original sense that enables us to discern good and evil. Its first precept: do good and avoid evil. Its principles include protecting life, family, truth, and seeking God. The natural law is universal and unchangeable, and is the basis for human rights. It is distinguished from the Old Law (the Ten Commandments), the New Law (the Gospel, the Beatitudes), and civil law. Thomas Aquinas defined law as ‘an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by the one who has care of the community, and promulgated.’ An unjust law is not truly law (St. Augustine, Martin Luther King Jr. citing Aquinas).”

Say: “The morality of human acts rests on three sources: the object chosen (what the act is), the intention (the end for which we do it), and the circumstances. For an act to be good, all three must be good. Some acts are intrinsically evil: ‘it is never allowed to do evil that good may come of it’ (Romans 3:8). This rules out, for example, murder of an innocent, adultery, and torture, regardless of intention. Conscience is the judgment by which we apply the law to a particular act. It can be formed or deformed. Mayer’s conscience told him he must preach; the law of the state said otherwise. He appealed to a higher law. Moral objectivity is key: the good is not just what we feel or what the majority says.”
ask: What is true freedom? (The power to do good, based on truth.)
What is natural law? (The moral law known by reason, written on the heart.)
What are the three sources of morality? (Object, intention, circumstances.)
practice: Run three cases through the three sources: lying to protect a friend; stealing to feed a family; breaking a promise to help someone.
For each, identify the object, intention and circumstances, and decide.
Write the difference between freedom and license in your own words.
Share a case where you struggled.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, make me free for the good.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Use the three sources to think through a decision this week.”

tryit: Distinguish freedom from license.
Run a case through the three sources of morality.
State the first precept of natural law.
lessons.saintStory:
Rupert Mayer was born in 1876 in Stuttgart, Germany. He became a Jesuit and was ordained in 1899. During World War I, he served as a chaplain on the front lines, where he lost his left leg to a grenade. He returned to Munich, a popular preacher, a pastor to the poor and to migrants, and a friend of workers.
In the 1920s he saw the rise of Nazism and denounced it. He preached against its racism, its hatred of the Church, and its violence. From 1937 he was forbidden to preach. He ignored the ban, because his conscience told him he could not be silent. He was arrested in 1937, imprisoned for seven months, then released. When he preached again, he was arrested in 1939 and sent to Sachsenhausen concentration camp. Fearing that his death would make him a martyr, the regime put him under house arrest in a monastery at Ettal.
He died on All Saints’ Day, 1945, while saying Mass, of a stroke. He was beatified in 1987.

lessons.title: Sin, virtue and grace
lessons.idea: Virtue is a habit of doing good; sin is the opposite. Grace is God’s free gift that heals and elevates us. Together they form the dynamic of the moral life: God’s grace, our response, virtues that grow, and the fruits of the Spirit.
lessons.question: How do we grow in virtue?
lessons.activity: “Make a plan” (35 min). Students identify one virtue to cultivate and one vice to resist. They design a habit plan: a daily practice, a support person, a prayer, a measure. They reflect on how grace will help.
teach: Virtues are habits of the soul (CCC 1803). The human virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance (CCC 1805–1809). Theological virtues: faith, hope, charity (CCC 1812–1829).
Grace is “favor, the free and undeserved help that God gives us” (CCC 1996). Sanctifying grace makes us holy; actual grace helps in particular acts (CCC 2000).
The gifts and fruits of the Holy Spirit complete the virtues (CCC 1830–1832). Merit is possible because grace is already at work (CCC 2006–2011).
Vice is the habit of sin. The seven capital sins and their remedies are a classic guide.
quiz: Virtues are…|Rules|Feelings|Inborn traits|Habits of the good acquired by practice and strengthened by grace (CCC 1803)|3|CCC 1803.
The theological virtues differ from the cardinal virtues because they…|Are optional|Are only for saints|Are easier|Have God for their object and are infused by him (CCC 1812–1813)|3|CCC 1812–1813.
Merit, in Catholic teaching, means that…|By grace God enables our good acts to be rewarded (CCC 2006–2009)|Faith alone is false|We earn grace by ourselves|Works are useless|0|CCC 2006–2011.
lessons.life: Track a virtue.
lessons.saint: John Climacus: the abbot whose Ladder of Divine Ascent charts the climb from vice to virtue.
lessons.mem: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)
lessons.hook: Read Galatians 5:22–23. Ask: “How do you recognize a person of virtue?” By the fruit, not just the rules.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe how grace and virtue work together with an example.

script.open: Show a ladder, or draw one. Ask, “What is the difference between falling off a ladder and never climbing one? Which is worse?” Take answers. “John Climacus says the spiritual life is a climb with many falls.”
teach: Say: “Grace is God’s free gift, his help to respond to his call and become his adopted children. The Catechism: ‘Grace is a participation in the life of God.’ (CCC 1997) Sanctifying grace is the habitual gift that makes us pleasing to God. Actual graces are God’s interventions at the start of conversion or in the course of sanctification. Sacramental graces are proper to each sacrament. Charisms are special gifts for the common good. Grace is first of all the gift of the Holy Spirit who justifies and sanctifies us. It is not earned: ‘For by grace you have been saved through faith.’ (Ephesians 2:8) Yet it requires cooperation: grace perfects nature but does not replace it. The saints show that grace can make weak people strong.”

Say: “Virtue. A virtue is ‘a habitual and firm disposition to do the good’ (CCC 1803). Human virtues are acquired by education, deliberate acts and perseverance. The four cardinal virtues: prudence (right reason in action), justice (giving to God and neighbor what is due), fortitude (firmness in difficulty), temperance (moderation of the attraction of pleasure). They are the hinges (cardo) of moral life. The three theological virtues, faith, hope and charity, are infused by God and have God as their object. They are given with grace. The gifts of the Holy Spirit and the fruits follow. Aristotle said we become just by doing just acts. Aquinas held that grace elevates virtue.”

Say: “Sin and vice. Vices are habits that incline us toward evil. The capital sins are pride, avarice, envy, wrath, lust, gluttony and sloth. Pride is the root. Each vice has an opposite virtue and remedy: pride and humility; avarice and generosity; envy and gratitude; wrath and patience; lust and chastity; gluttony and temperance; sloth and diligence (or zeal). Evagrius first described eight thoughts; Gregory the Great gave the list of seven. Practical program: examine daily; target a particular vice; do the opposite virtue in small acts; use the sacraments; accept correction; ask for help. Growth is slow: ‘Slowly, slowly, the light comes.’ The Ladder shows that falls are expected, and the key is to get up and go on.”
ask: What is grace? (Participation in God’s life; his free gift.)
What are the cardinal virtues? (Prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance.)
What is the root of all the capital sins? (Pride.)
practice: Make a table: vice, opposite virtue, specific daily action, who can help.
Fill in for all seven capital sins.
Honestly rate yourself 1-5 on each virtue.
Choose one to work on this month, with a daily action.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, give me the grace to climb.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Track one virtue for a week.”

tryit: Match each vice with its remedy.
Rate yourself honestly.
Choose one virtue and plan daily practice.
lessons.saintStory:
John was a monk who lived on Mount Sinai in the seventh century, in the monastery of St. Catherine. He entered as a teenager and lived as a hermit for many years in a cell near the foot of the mountain, where he studied the Fathers and prayed. Around the age of seventy-five, he was elected abbot of the monastery.
At the request of another abbot, John wrote The Ladder of Divine Ascent, a manual for monks. It describes thirty steps, like the rungs of Jacob’s ladder, from renouncing the world to love. The steps include obedience, repentance, remembrance of death, mourning, freedom from anger, humility, discernment, prayer and love. Along the way, he describes in detail the struggles with vices: vainglory, pride, anger, despair and others.
He died around 649. The book became hugely popular in the East, read every Lent in monasteries. His point: the spiritual life is a climb, with falls and recoveries, and virtue is built step by step. The monastic icon shows monks climbing a ladder while demons try to pull them down and angels help them.

units.title: The Commandments I: love of God

lessons.title: First commandment
lessons.idea: The first commandment, “You shall have no other gods before me,” commands faith, hope and charity and forbids superstition, idolatry, divination, atheism and tempting God. Worship belongs to God alone.
lessons.question: What are modern idols?
lessons.activity: “Reflect” (30 min). Students list modern “idols” and the signs of idolatry (time, devotion, sacrifices, identity). They write a short examination of their own lives: What could take first place in my heart? What is my plan to keep God first?
teach: The first commandment calls us to believe in God, hope in him and love him above all (CCC 2084–2094). Adoration, prayer, sacrifice and keeping promises are acts of worship (CCC 2096–2103).

Sins against it: doubt, unbelief, heresy, apostasy, schism (CCC 2088–2089); presumption, despair (CCC 2091–2092); superstition, idolatry, divination, magic, sacrilege, simony (CCC 2110–2128); atheism, agnosticism (CCC 2123–2128).
Images are not forbidden: Christ’s Incarnation makes holy images possible (CCC 2129–2132).
Idolatry today may take the form of power, pleasure, money or ideologies (CCC 2113).
quiz: Idolatry, as the Catechism describes it, is…|Giving to a creature the honor due to God alone, including money, power or pleasure (CCC 2113)|Only worship of statues|Prayer|Respect for saints|0|CCC 2113.
Which is a sin against the first commandment?|Missing a feast|Arguing|Sleeping|Tempting God and presumption, as well as despair, superstition and atheism (CCC 2110–2128)|3|CCC 2110–2128.

Veneration of holy images is legitimate because…|The Old Law allows it|They are magic|They are decorative|Christ is the image of the invisible God and honor passes to the person depicted (CCC 2132)|3|CCC 2131–2132.
lessons.life: Examine what you put first.
lessons.saint: The Maccabean mother and her seven sons: a family who refused to eat forbidden food and died rather than betray God.
lessons.mem: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might.” (Deuteronomy 6:5)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do people give their lives to?” (fame, money, success, relationships). Read Exodus 20:3 and introduce idolatry as putting a created good in God’s place.
lessons.assess: Ask students to identify three sins against the first commandment and give a modern example of idolatry.

script.open: Ask, “Name something that people today treat as if it were God: they organize their lives around it, give up anything for it, and look to it for happiness.” Write the answers. “The first commandment is about this.”
teach: Read Exodus 20:2-5 and Deuteronomy 6:4-5. Say: “‘I am the Lord your God… You shall have no other gods before me.’ And the Shema: ‘Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God is one Lord; and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might.’ The first commandment calls us to faith, hope and charity, and to worship. The Catechism connects it to the theological virtues: to believe in God, hope in him, love him above all. And adoration: to recognize God as Creator and Savior; prayer, sacrifice, keeping promises and vows made to him.”

Say: “Sins against the first commandment. Against faith: voluntary doubt, incredulity, heresy, apostasy, schism. Against hope: despair and presumption. Against charity: indifference, ingratitude, spiritual sloth, hatred of God. Superstition: attributing magical power to practices or objects (horoscopes, charms), or excess in devotion. Idolatry: giving divine honor to a creature: money, power, pleasure, sports, nation. Divination and magic: seeking to learn the future through occult means, tarot, mediums, or spiritism. Irreligion: tempting God, sacrilege, simony. Atheism and agnosticism: practical or theoretical. Modern idols: wealth, success, appearance, technology, political ideology, even the self.”

Say: “Images. The Church distinguishes between idols and sacred images. Since the Incarnation, Christians may represent Christ, Mary and the saints in icons, statues and paintings, which are reverenced but not adored (Nicaea II, 787). Adoration is for God alone. The first commandment calls us to an undivided heart. Jesus: ‘No one can serve two masters… You cannot serve God and mammon.’ (Matthew 6:24) The martyrs, like the Maccabees, show what it costs. And the first commandment is good news: God alone satisfies. Our heart is made for him. A practical examination: What do I think about most? What do I fear to lose? What would I sacrifice for? What do I turn to when anxious? The answers reveal what we worship.”
ask: What does the first commandment ask? (Faith, hope, love and adoration of God alone.)
Name two sins against it. (Idolatry, superstition, despair, presumption, atheism.)
What is the difference between an idol and an icon? (Idols receive divine honor; icons point to Christ and saints and are venerated.)
practice: List ten modern idols and the promise each makes.
For each, write what God offers that it can’t.
Do a personal inventory: what do I think about most, fear losing, sacrifice for?
Write a prayer of adoration and commitment.
script.close: Pray the Act of Faith, Hope and Love. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Fast from one idol for a day.”

tryit: Name the forms of idolatry today.
Find the root of each.
Compose a prayer of adoration.
lessons.saintStory:
In the second century before Christ, the Syrian king Antiochus IV Epiphanes tried to force the Jews to abandon their faith. He desecrated the Temple, banned circumcision and Sabbath, and ordered everyone to eat pork, which was forbidden by the Law. 2 Maccabees 7 tells of a mother and her seven sons, arrested and tortured.
One after the other, the sons refused. “We are ready to die rather than transgress the laws of our fathers.” The first had his tongue cut out; the second was scalped; each was killed with torment as the king looked on. Yet each spoke of the resurrection: “The King of the universe will raise us up to an everlasting renewal of life.” The mother encouraged each in their language: “I do not know how you came into being in my womb. It was not I who gave you life and breath… the Creator of the world will give life and breath back to you again.”
The youngest was last. The king tried to persuade him with promises of wealth. The mother urged him to accept death, “so that in God’s mercy I may get you back again with your brothers.” She died after her sons. The Church honors them as the Holy Maccabees.

lessons.title: Second and third commandments
lessons.idea: The second commandment commands reverence for God’s name, forbidding blasphemy, perjury and the misuse of oaths. The third commandment commands keeping the Lord’s Day holy by participating in Mass and resting from unnecessary work.
lessons.question: How do we keep Sunday?
lessons.activity: “Plan a Sunday” (35 min). Students plan a model Sunday that includes Mass, rest, family, service and leisure. They note obstacles (sports, work, screens) and solutions. Write a Sunday commitment.
teach: The second commandment: God’s name is holy (CCC 2142–2149). Blasphemy, profanity, false oaths and cursing are sins (CCC 2148–2155). Using God’s name in prayer and blessing honors it.
The third: Sunday is the Lord’s Day, commemorating the Resurrection (CCC 2174–2176). Sunday Mass is obligatory (CCC 2180–2183); rest, family, charity and leisure belong to the day (CCC 2184–2188).
Holy days of obligation in the United States: Mary Mother of God, Ascension, Assumption, All Saints, Immaculate Conception, Christmas (with the usual exceptions) (CCC 2043).
Excuses: illness, caring for infants and similar serious reasons (CCC 2181).
quiz: The second commandment forbids…|Reading|Singing|Praying aloud|Blasphemy, cursing and false oaths (CCC 2148–2155)|2|CCC 2148–2155.
Sunday Mass is obligatory because…|It keeps the Lord’s Day, the day of the Resurrection (CCC 2174, 2180)|It is a custom|Priests need attendance|Civil law|0|CCC 2174, 2180.
Rest on the Lord’s Day is intended to…|Free time for worship, family, works of mercy and leisure (CCC 2184–2188)|Avoid all activity|Be idle|Earn merit|0|CCC 2184–2188.
lessons.life: Keep Sunday as a day of rest.
lessons.saint: The martyrs of Abitene: forty-nine Christians who said, “We cannot live without the Lord’s Day.”
lessons.mem: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.” (Exodus 20:8)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What would you think if someone used your name as a curse?” Read Exodus 20:7–11. God’s name is holy.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain why God’s name is holy and how to keep Sunday holy.

script.open: Ask, “If the choice were Sunday Mass or an important game, what factors would decide it? What does your answer reveal about what’s first?” Take honest answers.
teach: Read Exodus 20:7-11. Say: “The second commandment: ‘You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.’ The name stands for the person. God revealed his name to Moses. The Catechism: ‘The second commandment prescribes respect for the Lord’s name.’ (CCC 2142) Sins against it: blasphemy (words against God, Christ, Mary, saints or the Church), cursing, careless oaths, false oaths, perjury, breaking vows. Using ‘Jesus Christ’ or ‘Oh my God’ as exclamations is disrespectful. The name of Jesus is the center of prayer: ‘There is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved.’ We bless God’s name: ‘Blessed be the name of the Lord.’ We begin prayers in the name of the Trinity. Our own name given at Baptism is sacred.”

Say: “The third commandment: ‘Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.’ The Sabbath is the seventh day, a day of rest commemorating creation (Exodus 20) and liberation from slavery (Deuteronomy 5). The early Christians moved their worship to Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, the first day of the week, ‘the Lord’s Day’ (Revelation 1:10). Acts 20:7: ‘On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread.’ Justin Martyr (AD 155) describes the Sunday Eucharist. Sunday is the ‘eighth day’ of the new creation. The Church requires Catholics to attend Mass on Sundays and holy days of obligation and to abstain from servile work and activities that hinder the joy and rest of the Lord’s day.”

Say: “Holy days of obligation in the U.S.: Mary, Mother of God (Jan 1), Ascension (Thursday or transferred to Sunday in most dioceses), Assumption (Aug 15), All Saints (Nov 1), Immaculate Conception (Dec 8), Christmas (Dec 25). The obligation binds under pain of grave sin unless excused by illness or serious cause. We keep Sunday by Mass, rest, family time, works of charity, and relaxation. Deliberately missing Mass without serious reason is a mortal sin because it cuts us off from the source of grace. Pope John Paul II’s Dies Domini (1998) calls Sunday ‘the day of the Lord, the day of Christ, the day of the Church, the day of humanity, the day of joy.’ The martyrs of Abitene show it’s not a mere obligation but a need.”
ask: What does the second commandment require? (Reverence for God’s name; no blasphemy or false oaths.)
Why do Christians keep Sunday? (It’s the day of the Resurrection.)
What is the Sunday obligation? (Attend Mass and refrain from unnecessary work.)
practice: Sort 10 uses of God’s name into reverent and irreverent.
Plan an ideal Lord’s Day: Mass, rest, family, service, with times.
Identify which obstacles you face (sports, work, screens) and how to handle them.
Write a short reflection on “Without Sunday we cannot live.”
script.close: Pray the Divine Praises: “Blessed be God. Blessed be his holy name.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Keep your next Sunday as a true Lord’s Day.”

tryit: Trace how the day of worship moved from Sabbath to Sunday.
Plan a Lord’s Day.
List reverent uses of God’s name.
lessons.saintStory:
In AD 304, under Emperor Diocletian, Christians were forbidden on pain of death from gathering for worship or keeping the Scriptures. In Abitene, a small town in North Africa, forty-nine Christians, including priests, women and a boy, were found celebrating the Sunday Eucharist in a private house. They were arrested and taken to Carthage for trial before the proconsul.
When questioned, one of them, Emeritus, in whose house they had met, answered, “Without the Lord’s Day, we cannot live.” (Sine dominico non possumus.) Another, Saturninus, said, “We celebrated the Lord’s Day, as our religion required.” They were tortured and imprisoned; many died in prison of hunger.
The account of their trial, preserved in Christian records, is one of the great early statements of the importance of Sunday. Their motto has been quoted by popes: for a Christian, the Sunday Mass is not an optional extra but the center of life.

lessons.title: Prayer as response
lessons.idea: Prayer is the response of the human heart to God, a living relationship. Whether vocal, meditative or contemplative, prayer is a gift God offers, and a battle we must fight. Luke 11:1: “Lord, teach us to pray.”
lessons.question: How do we pray?
lessons.activity: “Pray a Psalm” (35 min). Students pray Psalm 63 or 130 slowly in different ways: aloud together, silently, as a dialogue. Afterwards, they write a short reflection on what the Psalm says about prayer, and how they can pray it again this week.
teach: Prayer is “the raising of one’s mind and heart to God” (CCC 2559). It is a response to God’s initiative: “God thirsts that we may thirst for him” (CCC 2560).
Forms: blessing, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, praise (CCC 2626–2643). Expressions: vocal, meditation, contemplation (CCC 2700–2724).
The battle of prayer: distraction, dryness, discouragement, acedia. Persevere (CCC 2725–2745).
The place of prayer: the home, church, small spaces, nature. Time: daily, with the Church (CCC 2691–2699).
quiz: Prayer in the Catechism is…|A vital and personal relationship with the living God (CCC 2558)|A duty only|An emotion|A technique|0|CCC 2558.
The Church’s three expressions of prayer are…|Song, dance, speech|Morning, noon, night|Vocal, meditative and contemplative (CCC 2700–2724)|Public, private, silent|2|CCC 2700–2724.
Acedia, a “battle of prayer,” is…|Spiritual laziness or discouragement that tempts us to stop praying (CCC 2733)|A feast|A type of prayer|A sin of pride|0|CCC 2733.
lessons.life: Pray 15 minutes daily.
lessons.saint: Elizabeth of the Trinity: a young Carmelite who found God’s dwelling within.
misc: “If I am distracted, I am not praying.”
lessons.mem: “Lord, teach us to pray.” (Luke 11:1)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 11:1. Ask: “Why did the disciples ask this question? What did they see in Jesus’ prayer?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to name forms and expressions of prayer and an obstacle.

script.open: Ask, “How would you pray if you could not use words? What if you had to pray for five minutes in silence? Would you know how?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Prayer is a response to God who first calls us. The Catechism: ‘Prayer is the raising of one’s mind and heart to God or the requesting of good things from God.’ (CCC 2559) It is a covenant relationship, a communion. Three expressions: vocal prayer, meditation, contemplation. The sources: Scripture, liturgy, theological virtues. The way: the Holy Spirit is the teacher. Jesus taught us to pray: the Our Father is the summary of the Gospel. Prayer is both a gift and a battle: we need perseverance. Prayer is a school: we learn by doing.”

Say: “Forms. Blessing and adoration: we recognize God as God. Petition: we ask. Intercession: we ask for others. Thanksgiving. Praise. Methods. Lectio divina: read, meditate, pray, contemplate. Ignatian meditation: imagine the scene. The Jesus Prayer: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner,’ repeated in rhythm with breathing. The Rosary: vocal prayer with meditation. Centering prayer: silent attention to God. Adoration: silent presence before the Blessed Sacrament. The Liturgy of the Hours. Journaling. Walking prayer. Some are better at different times of life; the key is to find a method that helps you stay with God.”

Say: “Obstacles. Distractions: gently return. Dryness: continue anyway; fidelity matters more than feeling. Busy-ness: schedule a fixed time. Doubt: bring it to God. Sloth: begin small. Discouragement: remember that the desire to pray is itself a prayer. Elizabeth of the Trinity found God present within: ‘I have found my heaven on earth, since heaven is God and God is in my soul.’ We pray in hope and in the Spirit. Practical plan: a set time, a set place, a set length (begin with 10 minutes), a starting prayer (to the Holy Spirit), a Scripture passage, a time of silence, a closing prayer. Pray with others too, for the Church prays together. Prayer is the response to a love that comes first.”
ask: Name the three expressions of prayer. (Vocal, meditation, contemplation.)
What is the Jesus Prayer? (Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.)
What should we do with distractions? (Return gently.)
practice: Try lectio divina on a short Gospel passage for five minutes.
Try the Jesus Prayer for three minutes.
Sit in silence for two minutes.
Write which one helped you most and make a plan for a daily ten minutes.
script.close: Pray Elizabeth’s prayer “O my God, Trinity whom I adore” (a few lines). Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray ten minutes a day this week.”

tryit: Try three prayer methods.
Note what happens in each.
Pick a daily practice.
lessons.saintStory:
Élisabeth Catez was born in 1880 in France, in a military family. She was a spirited child, with a fierce temper, but in her teens she converted her will to love of Jesus. At fourteen, she made a private vow of virginity. She was a gifted pianist and enjoyed society. She longed to enter Carmel, but her mother refused until she turned twenty-one. Meanwhile, she lived like a nun at home, praying and serving.
In 1901 she entered the Carmel at Dijon. She had a deep sense of the indwelling of the Trinity, taught by Paul and John: “We will come to him and make our home with him.” Her prayer, “O my God, Trinity whom I adore,” expresses her sense of living in constant awareness of God’s presence in the soul.
She fell ill with Addison’s disease, a painful illness, and died in 1906, at twenty-six. She suffered with joy and called herself “Laudem Gloriae,” praise of glory. She was canonized in 2016.

units.title: The Commandments II: love of neighbor

lessons.title: Life and chastity
lessons.idea: The fifth commandment protects the dignity of human life from conception to natural death; the sixth, with the ninth, protects the dignity of the person in sexuality through chastity. Both defend persons from being used.
lessons.question: What does the Church teach about chastity?
lessons.activity: “Respectful conversation” (40 min). With ground rules (listen, no mocking, optional sharing), students discuss: How do culture and media portray sex and violence? What does a life-giving view look like? Individually write a personal commitment to treat others as persons, not objects.
teach: The fifth commandment forbids murder and teaches respect for human life (CCC 2258–2317). Abortion, euthanasia, suicide are grave offenses (CCC 2270–2283). Legitimate defense, war and the death penalty have strict limits (CCC 2263–2267, 2307–2317).
Chastity is the integration of sexuality within the person (CCC 2337). All are called to chastity according to their state: married, single, consecrated (CCC 2348–2350).

Offenses against chastity include lust, masturbation, pornography, fornication, prostitution, rape, adultery, homosexual acts, contraception (CCC 2351–2357, 2380–2391). Teach with charity and clarity.
Forgiveness, mercy and help are always available (CCC 1429).
talk: How do we speak with compassion?
quiz: Chastity is…|Repression of sexuality|A vow only for priests|The integration of sexuality within the person for the gift of self (CCC 2337)|Avoidance of others|2|CCC 2337.
The fifth commandment forbids…|Medicine|Spanking|The direct and intentional killing of the innocent (CCC 2268)|Self-defense in all cases|2|CCC 2258–2269.
Why does the Church link the body to the person?|It is a possession|It is evil|It is a machine|Body and soul form one person, so the body expresses the person (CCC 362–365, 2332)|3|CCC 362–365.
lessons.life: Read CCC 2331–2359.
lessons.saint: Jérôme Lejeune: the geneticist who discovered the cause of Down syndrome and spent his life defending those with it.
lessons.mem: “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.” (Genesis 1:27)
lessons.hook: Read Psalm 139:13–16 and Genesis 1:27. Ask: “How does it change how you treat people if each is made in the image of God?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain why life and chastity are connected to human dignity.

script.open: Ask, “Is a baby in the womb a human being? How would a scientist answer? A philosopher? A theologian?” Take answers. Write the points of agreement.
teach: Read Exodus 20:13 and Psalm 139. Say: “‘You shall not kill.’ The fifth commandment protects the life of the innocent. The Catechism: ‘Human life is sacred because from its beginning it involves the creative action of God and it remains forever in a special relationship with the Creator, who is its sole end.’ (CCC 2258) Only God is the Lord of life from its beginning until its end. Intentional killing of an innocent person is gravely wrong. Legitimate defense of self or others is allowed, even by lethal force if necessary, since the aim is to protect life; so is a just war under strict conditions (just cause, last resort, legitimate authority, probability of success, proportionality, right intention). The Catechism now teaches that the death penalty is inadmissible, because it is an attack on the dignity of the person (2018 revision).”

Say: “Beginning of life. The Church holds that human life must be respected from conception. Embryo is a human life with potential, not a potential human life. Abortion, direct and intentional, is gravely wrong. IVF raises concerns: it separates procreation from the marital act, often involves creating and discarding embryos. Embryonic stem-cell research destroys embryos. Adult stem cells and ethical research are encouraged. Prenatal diagnosis is allowed if it serves the child’s good but not if it leads to elimination. Eugenics is condemned. Infertility is a real cross; the Church supports ethical methods like NaProTechnology, and the option of adoption.”

Say: “Respect of the body. Torture, kidnapping, terrorism and mutilation are wrong. Drug abuse and excessive drinking are wrong; so are reckless driving and other risks. Medical research must respect persons. Organ donation can be an act of charity if done with consent and not hastening death. Caring for the weak is a duty. The fifth commandment extends to anger and hatred: Jesus said, ‘Everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment.’ Scandal, leading others to sin, is also a sin against this commandment. Peace: ‘Blessed are the peacemakers.’ Positive: protect life, welcome the vulnerable, build peace. Lejeune summed it up: ‘The quality of a civilization is measured by the respect it has for its weakest members.’”
ask: What does the fifth commandment protect? (Innocent human life.)
What are conditions for just war? (Just cause, last resort, legitimate authority, proportionality, probability of success, right intention.)
What does the Catechism now say of the death penalty? (It is inadmissible.)
practice: Write a case for the dignity of every human life using Scripture, science and reason.
List three objections you have heard and write replies.
Identify one action you can take to support life: volunteering, praying, advocating.
Write a prayer for the vulnerable.
script.close: Pray the Prayer for Life or Psalm 139. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for someone who is vulnerable.”

tryit: Make a case for the dignity of every human life.
Anticipate three objections.
Write your replies.
lessons.saintStory:
Jérôme Lejeune was born in 1926 in France. He became a physician and a geneticist. In 1958-59, working with Marthe Gautier and Raymond Turpin, he discovered that Down syndrome is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21. It was the first time a disability had been linked to a chromosome. He hoped it would lead to a cure.
Instead, as prenatal tests developed, he saw that the discovery was used to detect and abort children with the condition. He spoke out, at great professional cost. He lost research funding and honors, and received hate mail. He told the story of a young patient who asked him to find a cure, and he said that the greatest scandal was a “medicine that kills the patient to cure the disease.”
He testified at courts and gave lectures worldwide, calling every human being a person from conception. John Paul II made him the first president of the Pontifical Academy for Life in 1994, and he died a few weeks later. His cause for canonization is open; he is a Servant of God.

lessons.title: Justice and truth
lessons.idea: The seventh commandment forbids theft and commands justice in property, work and the care of the poor; the eighth commands truthfulness and forbids lying, calumny and detraction. Together they build trust in society.
lessons.question: How can we practice honesty?
lessons.activity: “Case studies” (40 min). Students study cases: cheating on a test, using pirated media, a business with unfair wages, spreading a rumor, keeping a secret. For each: which commandment, what justice requires, what repair is needed (restitution, apology).
teach: The seventh commandment: respect for others’ goods; the universal destination of goods and private property (CCC 2401–2418). Sins: theft, fraud, unjust wages, gambling abuse, cheating (CCC 2408–2414).
The Church’s social teaching: just wages, care for creation, solidarity with the poor (CCC 2426–2463).
The eighth: truth, witness and honesty (CCC 2464–2513). Sins: lying, perjury, rash judgment, detraction, calumny, flattery, boasting (CCC 2475–2487). Professional secrecy and the seal are protected.
Restitution is required when we harm others (CCC 2487).
quiz: Restitution is required when…|There is a lawsuit|A person has unjustly taken or damaged another’s goods (CCC 2412)|It is easy|Someone feels guilty|1|CCC 2412.
Detraction is…|Lying under oath|Complimenting|Disclosing without objectively valid reason another’s faults to those who did not know them (CCC 2477)|Telling the truth|2|CCC 2477.

The universal destination of goods means…|Wealth is evil|Earth’s goods are meant for the whole human family, and private property carries a social duty (CCC 2402–2406)|Property is illegal|Everything is shared equally|1|CCC 2402–2406.
lessons.life: Make restitution where needed.
lessons.saint: Rutilio Grande: a Salvadoran Jesuit who spoke for farm workers and was shot for it.
misc: “Small lies and small thefts don’t matter.”
lessons.mem: “Let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.” (Amos 5:24)
lessons.hook: Read Amos 5:24. Ask: “How does a society fall apart when no one tells the truth or respects property?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to analyze a scenario using the seventh and eighth commandments.

script.open: Ask, “Is it wrong to take what is not yours? Always? What about a loaf of bread to feed a starving family? What about a company that pays less than a living wage?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The seventh commandment, ‘You shall not steal,’ requires respect for others’ goods and the universal destination of goods. The Catechism says: ‘The seventh commandment forbids theft… that is, usurping another’s property against the reasonable will of the owner.’ (CCC 2408) It also forbids unjust wages, price-fixing, corruption, fraud, vandalism, gambling that cheats, exploitation of workers, tax evasion and sloth. Rights of private property are legitimate, but they have a social function. ‘The earth is the Lord’s.’ We are stewards. Restitution: one who has stolen must return what was taken. The principle of necessity: someone in extreme need may take what is necessary to survive.”

Say: “Work. The Church teaches the dignity of work: work is for the person, not the person for work. Workers have rights: to a just wage, rest, safe conditions, to form unions. Employers have duties. Pope Leo XIII, Rerum Novarum; John Paul II, Laborem Exercens. The economy must serve the common good. Special concern for the poor: preferential option for the poor. Defrauding laborers is a sin that ‘cries out to heaven’ (James 5:4). Also consumerism and greed. Pope Francis: ‘This economy kills.’ But the Church does not endorse any specific system; it tests every system against human dignity.”

Say: “The eighth commandment, ‘You shall not bear false witness,’ requires truth and honesty. Truth: a virtue of being true in deed and speech. The Catechism: ‘Lying consists in speaking a falsehood with the intention of deceiving.’ (CCC 2482) Sins include lying, perjury, rash judgment, detraction, calumny, flattery, boasting and breach of confidence. Reparation: one who has harmed another’s reputation must repair it. Professional secrecy is binding, and the seal of confession is absolute. Media: the right to information is limited by truth and charity. Beauty and art also express truth. Witness: martyrs bear witness to the truth. Rutilio Grande’s justice and truth: he named the lie of an unjust order and paid the cost. Jesus: ‘I am the way, and the truth, and the life.’”
ask: What does the seventh commandment forbid? (Theft, fraud, unjust wages, corruption, exploitation.)
What is the universal destination of goods? (God gave the earth for all.)
What does the eighth commandment require? (Truthfulness; reparation for harm to reputation.)
practice: Prepare cases: a store clerk gives too much change; a company underpays workers; a student spreads a rumor; a journalist publishes a half-truth.
For each, identify the commandment, the sin, and the remedy (restitution, correction, apology).
Choose a just cause you can support and write a plan.
Write a personal commitment to truthfulness.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, make me just and truthful.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Make a restitution or apology you owe.”

tryit: Apply the seventh and eighth commandments to a case.
Identify the duty of restitution.
Plan a just action.
lessons.saintStory:
Rutilio Grande was born in 1928 in El Salvador, in a poor family. He became a Jesuit, and after ordination he served in rural parishes. In the town of Aguilares, he organized the farm workers to discuss the Bible and their lives. Most of the land was owned by a few wealthy families, and the workers earned little. Rutilio taught that they had dignity as children of God and a right to a just wage and decent conditions.
His preaching angered the landowners and the military government. In a famous sermon in 1977, he said that if Jesus were to come back, they would arrest and crucify him again for his message. A month later, on March 12, 1977, he was driving to a village for Mass with an elderly man and a teenage boy. Gunmen opened fire and killed all three.
The killing changed Archbishop Oscar Romero, who had been quiet. He insisted on a single funeral Mass for Rutilio, closing every other Mass in the country. Rutilio was beatified in 2022.

lessons.title: Desire and detachment
lessons.idea: The ninth and tenth commandments reach the heart: purity of heart and detachment from possessions. “Blessed are the pure in heart.” They teach us to guard desires and to be generous and content.
lessons.question: What does purity of heart mean?
lessons.activity: “Reflection” (30 min). Students journal on: What do I envy? What do I covet? How do I guard my heart (media, friendships, gratitude)? They choose one practical step toward purity of heart and one toward generosity.
teach: The ninth commandment: purity of heart; battles against lust through modesty, discipline of the senses and prayer (CCC 2514–2533). The tenth: detachment from riches and envy (CCC 2534–2557).
Envy is sadness at another’s good; avarice, a desire for wealth. The remedy is gratitude, generosity and trust in providence (CCC 2538–2540, 2544–2547).
“Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3) points to the freedom of detachment. “Where your treasure is, there will be your heart also” (Matthew 6:21).
Modesty protects intimacy and human dignity (CCC 2521–2524).
talk: How do we grow in detachment?
quiz: The tenth commandment targets…|Poverty|All desire|Desires that lead to unjust acquisition and envy (CCC 2534–2540)|Work|2|CCC 2534–2540.
Envy is…|Charity|Sadness at another’s good and the desire to possess it unjustly (CCC 2539)|Joy in another’s good|Healthy competition|1|CCC 2539.
“Blessed are the pure in heart” points toward…|Single-minded love of God and purity of intention and desire (CCC 2518)|A rule|Isolation|Perfectionism|0|CCC 2518–2519.
lessons.life: Practice detachment: fast from a pleasure.
lessons.saint: Giuseppe Moscati: a Naples doctor who treated the poor free and left a fortune of love.
lessons.mem: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” (Matthew 5:8)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 5:8 and 5:28. Ask: “Why does Jesus say sin begins in the heart?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe the difference between wants and covetousness and one remedy.

script.open: Ask, “Name a thing you wanted for months. When you got it, how long did it satisfy you? What does this say about wanting?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The ninth commandment: ‘You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.’ The tenth: ‘You shall not covet your neighbor’s goods.’ They guard the heart, because sin begins within. Jesus said, ‘From within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, fornication, theft, murder, adultery, coveting…’ (Mark 7:21-22) The ninth commandment concerns purity of heart: the struggle against lust; custody of the senses and the imagination; modesty; purity of intention and speech. The tenth forbids greed and envy. The Catechism says the two commandments ‘require that we strive for purity of heart and detachment.’”

Say: “Purity of heart: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.’ It is a gift and a work. How to cultivate: prayer, sacraments, discipline of the eyes and the imagination, avoiding occasions, modesty in dress and behavior, healthy friendships. Modesty protects the intimate center of the person and respects the dignity of others. It also affects what we watch and share. Detachment from goods: poverty of spirit. Not necessarily having nothing, but freedom from clinging. Envy: sadness at another’s good. A cure is gratitude and rejoicing in others’ gifts. Greed: the desire for more. A cure is generosity, almsgiving and simplicity.”

Say: “Desire itself is not evil. We are made for infinite goodness. The problem is disordered desire. The Church says our desires, rightly ordered, lead to God. Augustine: ‘Our heart is restless until it rests in thee.’ Aquinas: happiness consists in seeing God. We should direct our desires: to ask what I truly want, and whether this will lead there. Moscati: he had success and wealth available, but chose service. Practical steps: a regular fast; give away something you value; spend time without screens; thank God daily for what you have; avoid comparison online; give to those in need. Philippians 4:11-13: ‘I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content.’ Ask for the gift of a clean heart.”
ask: What do the ninth and tenth commandments guard? (The heart; purity and detachment.)
What is modesty? (Protecting the intimate center of the person and respecting others.)
What is the cure for envy? (Gratitude and rejoicing in others’ good.)
practice: List five things you strongly desire.
For each, ask: Why do I want it? Will it satisfy? Does it lead me closer to God?
Choose one thing to give up or give away this week.
Write three things you are grateful for.
script.close: Pray: “Create in me a clean heart, O God.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Practice one act of detachment.”

tryit: Examine your desires.
Find the root of each.
Practice one detachment.
lessons.saintStory:
Giuseppe Moscati was born in 1880 in Benevento, Italy. He studied medicine in Naples, and became a physician, researcher and professor. He was a renowned scientist, publishing papers and making discoveries in the chemistry of glycogen. In 1906, when Mount Vesuvius erupted, he rushed to evacuate patients from a hospital before the roof collapsed. During a cholera outbreak, and in World War I, he worked tirelessly.
He treated the poor without charge, and even left money under their prescriptions to help them buy medicine. Rich patients were charged, and sometimes he sent them away if they were too rude. He went to Mass every morning. He lived simply with his sister, never married, and believed medicine was a vocation to serve Christ in the sick.
He taught his students: “Love is the only thing that can transform man. Not science, but charity.” He died in 1927, at forty-six, after a day of seeing patients. Crowds of poor people lined the streets for his funeral. He was canonized in 1987.

units.title: Social teaching and conscience in action
units.eq: What does it mean to love in society?

lessons.title: Human dignity and the common good
lessons.idea: Catholic social teaching begins with the dignity of the human person, who is the foundation, cause and goal of social life. The common good is the sum of conditions that allow people to flourish. Subsidiarity and participation protect freedom.
lessons.question: What is the common good?
lessons.activity: “Case study” (40 min). Present a local issue (a closing factory, a refugee family, a neighborhood without a grocery store). Students apply the principles: dignity, common good, subsidiarity, participation, solidarity. Propose practical actions and who should act.
teach: Society exists for the person (CCC 1877–1885). The common good: “the sum total of social conditions which allow people… to reach their fulfillment more fully and more easily” (CCC 1906).
Subsidiarity: larger bodies should not take over what smaller communities can do (CCC 1883–1885). Participation allows all to contribute (CCC 1913–1917).
Authority serves the common good (CCC 1897–1904). The state must protect human rights (CCC 1907–1912).
Rerum Novarum (1891), Quadragesimo Anno, Mater et Magistra, Gaudium et Spes, Centesimus Annus and Laudato Si’ develop these themes.
talk: What is the role of authority?
quiz: The common good is…|The sum of social conditions that allow people to reach their fulfillment (CCC 1906)|The majority’s preference|Only economic output|Whatever the government decides|0|CCC 1906.
Subsidiarity guards against…|Charity|Local control|Absorbing the proper roles of smaller communities into larger ones (CCC 1883)|All government|3|CCC 1883–1885.
The dignity of the person is, in Catholic social teaching, the…|Political party|Opinion|Last principle|Foundation of all the others|3|CCC 1700–1709, 1929.
lessons.life: Vote and engage thoughtfully.
lessons.saint: Giorgio La Pira: a mayor of Florence who treated housing, work and peace as sacred duties.
misc: “Catholic social teaching belongs to one political party.”
“The Church should stay out of public life.”
lessons.mem: “So God created man in his own image.” (Genesis 1:27)
lessons.hook: Read Genesis 1:27. Ask: “How does this verse apply to laws about work, housing, health?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to define the common good and subsidiarity and apply them to a case.

script.open: Ask, “What does a good society need that no individual can build alone? Make a list: roads, courts, schools, clean water, safety. Who is responsible?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Catholic social teaching rests on a vision of the human person in community. The Compendium of the Social Doctrine of the Church states key principles. The dignity of the human person: the foundation. The common good: ‘the sum total of social conditions which allow people, either as groups or as individuals, to reach their fulfillment more fully and more easily.’ (GS 26) It has three elements: respect for the person and basic rights; social well-being and development of the group; and peace, the stability and security of a just order. The common good is not the good of the majority, nor the sum of individual interests. It is a good that is shared by all.”

Say: “Other principles. The universal destination of goods: God gave creation for all, so property has a social function. Subsidiarity: a higher body should not take over what a lower one can do; decisions are made at the level closest to the people affected, and the higher gives help when needed. Participation: everyone has a right and duty to take part in social life. Solidarity: ‘a firm and persevering determination to commit oneself to the common good’ (John Paul II, Sollicitudo Rei Socialis 38). Together, they form a vision between individualism, which ignores community, and collectivism, which neglects the person.”

Say: “The State has a role: to promote the common good, defend rights, maintain order and justice. The Church teaches that political authority comes from God through the natural law and must serve the people. Citizens have duties: to pay taxes, vote, defend the country, obey just laws. We do not obey unjust laws (Acts 5:29). Catholics in politics: the Church doesn’t endorse parties but insists that Catholics form their conscience by the Gospel. Pope Benedict said that politics is ‘the primary way of charity.’ Paul VI called it ‘a demanding form of charity.’ La Pira lived this. In the U.S., the bishops’ ‘Faithful Citizenship’ sets out principles. Catholics must weigh issues, with intrinsic evils like abortion having priority along with concern for poverty, immigration, the environment and war.”
ask: What is the common good? (The social conditions that let all flourish.)
What is subsidiarity? (Decisions are made at the level closest to the people affected.)
What is solidarity? (Firm commitment to the good of all.)
practice: Choose a local issue: a school lunch policy, a park, a housing question.
Analyze it with four principles: dignity, common good, subsidiarity, solidarity.
Write what each principle would recommend.
Write a letter to a local official or plan a service.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, make us builders of the common good.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read one section of Faithful Citizenship.”

tryit: Define the common good.
Apply it to a school or town decision.
List its three elements.
lessons.saintStory:
Giorgio La Pira was born in 1904 in Sicily, to a poor family. He studied law, became a professor, and was a lay Dominican who prayed daily and went to Mass every morning. He lived simply and gave away his salary.
He was elected mayor of Florence in 1951. When a factory was about to close, throwing hundreds out of work, he intervened: he requisitioned buildings for the homeless, helped factories remain open, and built public housing. He took a strong stand for peace. He organized conferences of mayors from around the world and traveled to Moscow, Washington and Hanoi, advocating dialogue. He hosted gatherings of Mediterranean leaders in Florence, including Jews, Muslims and Christians.
His motto: politics is “the highest form of charity.” He died in 1977. His cause for canonization is open; he was declared Venerable in 2018.

lessons.title: Solidarity and the poor
lessons.idea: Solidarity is the firm commitment to the good of all, because we are responsible for one another. The preferential love for the poor reflects Christ’s identification with them: “As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.”
lessons.question: What is the option for the poor?
lessons.activity: “Service reflection” (40 min). Students plan and carry out (or reflect on) a service experience: serving a meal, tutoring, visiting the elderly. They reflect: What did I see? Who is invisible? What is one structural cause and one personal action?
teach: Solidarity is a social virtue and Christian love (CCC 1939–1942). John Paul II: not “a feeling of vague compassion” but “a firm and persevering determination to commit oneself to the common good.”
The preferential option for the poor (CCC 2443–2449): the poor are first in God’s love, and works of mercy are required (CCC 2447).
Charity and justice go together: giving to the poor is “a duty of justice” (CCC 2446). Almsgiving, volunteering and advocacy are all needed.
Pope Francis: “a Church that is poor and for the poor.”
quiz: Solidarity is…|A firm and persevering determination to commit oneself to the common good (John Paul II; CCC 1939–1942)|A tax|Charity only|A vague feeling of sympathy|0|CCC 1939–1942.

The “preferential option for the poor” means…|Poverty is holy|The poor have priority in the Church’s concern and our service (CCC 2443–2448)|Rich people are excluded|Ignoring the rich|1|CCC 2443–2448.
Matthew 25:31–46 teaches that final judgment depends on…|Wealth|Ritual only|Doctrine only|How we treated “the least of these” (CCC 1038, 2447)|3|Matthew 25:40.
lessons.life: Volunteer with the poor.
lessons.saint: Martin de Porres: a Peruvian brother who treated the sick of every race and class.
misc: “Poverty is always the poor person’s fault.”
lessons.mem: “As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” (Matthew 25:40)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 25:31–46. Ask: “What is the criterion of the final judgment? What surprised the people?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain solidarity and the preferential option for the poor with an example.

script.open: Ask, “If a stranger fell sick on your street, who would be responsible? Neighbors, government, charities? What about a stranger in another country?” Take answers.
teach: Read Luke 10:25-37. Say: “A lawyer asked, ‘Who is my neighbor?’ and Jesus told the story of the Good Samaritan. The Samaritan, an outsider and a hated foreigner, stopped when the priest and the Levite passed by. He bandaged the man, took him to an inn, paid, and promised to return. Jesus asked, ‘Which of these three was neighbor?’ and said, ‘Go and do likewise.’ Solidarity means we recognize all people as neighbors, and take responsibility for them. The Catechism: ‘The principle of solidarity… is also articulated in terms of friendship or social charity.’ (CCC 1939)”

Say: “The preferential option for the poor is the Church’s teaching that we give special attention to the needs of the poor and vulnerable. It’s not exclusive; it’s a priority. Scripture: God hears the cry of the poor (Exodus 3), the prophets denounce oppression, Jesus is born poor, announces good news to the poor (Luke 4), identifies with them (Matthew 25). The Church has always served the poor: deacons, hospitals, orphanages, soup kitchens, schools. The works of mercy summarize. John Paul II: ‘Love for the poor is incompatible with an immoderate love of riches.’ Poverty has many forms: material, spiritual, relational. The Church also teaches about justice for immigrants and refugees: the Holy Family were refugees in Egypt.”

Say: “Charity and justice. Charity meets immediate needs: feeding the hungry. Justice addresses causes: why are people hungry? Both are needed. ‘When I give food to the poor, they call me a saint. When I ask why the poor have no food, they call me a communist.’ (Dom Hélder Câmara) Catholic organizations: Catholic Charities, St. Vincent de Paul Society, Catholic Relief Services, Caritas, Habitat-type groups, and Catholic Worker houses. Practical solidarity: volunteer, give, advocate, buy fairly, welcome the stranger, and see the person. Dorothy Day said, ‘Our problems stem from our acceptance of this filthy, rotten system.’ Martin’s approach: see Christ in each person. Pope Francis: ‘The poor are not a problem; they are a resource.’ And we are all poor before God.”
ask: What does solidarity mean? (Taking responsibility for all as neighbors.)
What is the preferential option for the poor? (Special priority for the needs of the poor.)
What’s the difference between charity and justice? (Charity meets needs; justice addresses causes.)
practice: Choose a Catholic charity (Catholic Charities, CRS, St. Vincent de Paul) and research what it does.
Sort its activities into charity and justice.
Plan an act of solidarity: a drive, a visit, a letter, or advocacy.
Write what personal sacrifice it will take.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, let me see you in the poor.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Do one concrete act of service this week.”

tryit: Evaluate a charity by the works of mercy.
Distinguish charity from justice.
Plan an act of solidarity.
lessons.saintStory:
Martin de Porres was born in Lima, Peru, in 1579, the son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed Black woman from Panama. His father abandoned them, and Martin grew up in poverty. In that colonial society, he faced racism. He was apprenticed to a barber-surgeon, learning how to cut hair and care for the sick.
At fifteen, he joined the Dominican convent in Lima as a servant. He was not allowed to be a full brother because of his race. After years of devoted service, in 1603 the Dominicans accepted him. He cared for the sick in the infirmary, including the poor, slaves and nobles alike. Stories say that he healed through prayer and kindness. He fed the poor from the convent kitchen, and begged for them. He cared for stray animals. He started an orphanage and a school.
He died in 1639. When the viceroy came to venerate his body, the crowds were enormous. He was canonized in 1962 and is the patron of social justice and interracial harmony.

lessons.title: Creation and stewardship
lessons.idea: God entrusted creation to us as stewards. We must care for it with respect for its integrity, for the good of all and for future generations. Laudato Si’ calls for an “integral ecology” linking care for creation with care for the poor.
lessons.question: How can we care for creation?
lessons.activity: “Environmental project” (45 min). Students plan and start a project: reduce waste at school, plant a garden, organize a clean-up, audit energy use. Define goal, steps, partners and a prayer. Include reading excerpts from Laudato Si’.
teach: Creation is a gift with its own goodness (CCC 339–341). The seventh commandment requires respect for the integrity of creation (CCC 2415–2418).
Animals are to be treated kindly but not equal to persons (CCC 2416–2418). Resources are for all, now and in the future.
Laudato Si’ (2015) calls for “ecological conversion,” links environmental degradation with injustice to the poor and asks for lifestyle changes (the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor).
St Francis of Assisi is patron of ecology. The Canticle of the Creatures is a good prayer.
quiz: Laudato Si’ calls for an “integral ecology” meaning…|Ignoring people|Protecting trees only|Opposing industry|Connecting care for creation with justice for the poor and human dignity|3|Pope Francis, 2015.
Stewardship means…|Caring for creation as a gift entrusted to us for all (CCC 2415)|Leaving nature alone|Owning creation absolutely|Using resources freely|0|CCC 2415–2418.
The Catechism says animals…|May be used cruelly|Have no value|Equal humans|Are entrusted to our care but not equal to persons (CCC 2416–2418)|3|CCC 2416–2418.
lessons.life: Make an ecological commitment.
lessons.saint: Cuthbert: a hermit bishop who lived among seabirds and seals on a northern island.
misc: “Dominion means we can use creation however we like.”
lessons.mem: “The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to till it and keep it.” (Genesis 2:15)
lessons.hook: Read Genesis 2:15 (“to till it and keep it”). Ask: “What does it mean to be a gardener, not an owner?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain Catholic stewardship and propose a concrete action.

script.open: Ask, “What is one place in nature that you love? What would you feel if it were destroyed?” Take answers. “The Church has a lot to say about caring for it.”
teach: Read Genesis 1:26-31 and 2:15. Say: “God made the world and saw that it was good. He gave humans ‘dominion,’ but also placed man in the garden ‘to till it and keep it.’ Dominion is not domination but responsible stewardship. We are creatures among creatures. The Catechism: ‘The seventh commandment enjoins respect for the integrity of creation.’ (CCC 2415) Animals are entrusted to our stewardship, may be used for food and clothing and for medical research within reasonable limits, but it is contrary to human dignity to cause animals to suffer needlessly.”

Say: “Pope Francis’s encyclical Laudato Si’ (2015), ‘On Care for Our Common Home,’ draws on St. Francis’s Canticle of the Creatures. Its main themes: the world is a gift; there is an ecological crisis that is also a human and moral crisis: climate change, water pollution, loss of biodiversity, throwaway culture; the root is a ‘technocratic paradigm’ and consumerism that ignore limits; the poor suffer most; we need ‘integral ecology’ connecting care for nature with justice for the poor; and ‘ecological conversion.’ He wrote: ‘We must hear both the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor.’ Pope Benedict called for similar attention, and John Paul II named the ‘ecological crisis’ a moral issue.”

Say: “Responses. Personal: reduce waste, reuse, recycle, conserve energy and water, eat thoughtfully, avoid overconsumption, appreciate nature, give thanks. Communal: parish ‘Laudato Si’ circles, community gardens, advocacy for policies that protect creation and the poor. The Church doesn’t endorse particular policies, but asks for prudence and concern. There is debate about the science and policies; the Church affirms a moral duty to care for creation, and calls for dialogue based on the best science. Sabbath rest also teaches limits, a counter to endless production. The liturgy uses creation: water, oil, bread, wine, fire, incense. The Season of Creation (September 1 to October 4) is observed by many Christians. Cuthbert’s ducks: a small act can be a start. Psalm 24:1: ‘The earth is the Lord’s and the fullness thereof.’”
ask: What does stewardship mean? (Responsible care for creation entrusted to us.)
What is integral ecology? (Linking care for creation with justice for the poor.)
What did Francis say we must hear? (The cry of the earth and the cry of the poor.)
practice: Read three paragraphs from Laudato Si’ (e.g., 1-2, 13, 49).
List five personal actions and three community actions for creation care.
Choose one you will do this month and write how you will check it.
Write a short prayer of thanks for creation.
script.close: Pray the Canticle of the Creatures (a few lines). Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Take one concrete step for creation.”

tryit: Read Genesis 1-2 and Laudato Si’.
List duties of stewardship.
Plan a concrete action.
lessons.saintStory:
Cuthbert was born around 634 in northern England. As a young shepherd, he saw a vision of angels carrying a soul to heaven, which led him to enter the monastery at Melrose. He became prior of Lindisfarne, the island monastery. He traveled to remote villages on foot or horseback, preaching and teaching the people in their own dialect.
In 676 he withdrew to the tiny island of Inner Farne, where he lived as a hermit. He prayed and worked, growing barley with his hands. The Venerable Bede tells that Cuthbert would stand in the sea, praying through the night, and that, afterward, sea otters came out of the water to warm and dry his feet. He protected the eider ducks on the island, which became known as “Cuddy’s ducks.” Some of the oldest wildlife protection laws in Europe are said to go back to him.
He was drawn out of solitude to be bishop of Lindisfarne in 685. After two years, he returned to Inner Farne and died in 687.

units.title: Hard questions: marriage, family and suffering
units.eq: How does the Church walk with people in difficult situations?

lessons.title: Divorce and annulment
lessons.idea: Marriage is a permanent bond. The Church does not recognize divorce as ending a valid marriage, but an annulment can declare that a valid marriage never existed, and divorced Catholics are still part of the Church.
lessons.question: Is annulment just Catholic divorce?
lessons.activity: Study the steps of an annulment and the questions a tribunal asks.
teach: Jesus taught that what God has joined together no one should separate (Mark 10:9; CCC 2382). A valid, consummated sacramental marriage can be dissolved only by death (CCC 1638–1640).

An annulment is a finding that the marriage was never valid, for example because of a lack of freedom, serious incapacity or intention (CCC 1629). It does not make children illegitimate and is not a verdict on blame.

Divorced Catholics are not excommunicated. Those who remarry without an annulment cannot receive Communion, but the Church asks that they be welcomed, prayed for and helped (CCC 1651; Amoris Laetitia, 2016).
Separation may be necessary for safety (CCC 1649), especially in cases of abuse. The Church never asks someone to stay in danger.
talk: What are the risks to a family when marriage is treated as temporary?
Why might someone feel judged by the Church after a divorce?
How can a parish accompany people in broken marriages?
quiz: What does an annulment declare?|That a valid marriage never existed|That children are illegitimate|That one spouse is guilty|That a marriage has ended|0|CCC 1629.
A divorced Catholic who has not remarried…|May receive the sacraments|Must leave the Church|May not attend Mass|Is excommunicated|0|CCC 1651.
When may spouses separate?|Only with a bishop’s permission|Never|When necessary, such as for safety|When they disagree|2|CCC 1649.
lessons.life: Pray for a family you know that is struggling. Offer practical help.
lessons.saint: Rita of Cascia: a wife in a violent marriage, a mother, a widow and a sister, who prayed for peace.
misc: “An annulment is just a Catholic divorce.”
lessons.mem: “What therefore God has joined together, let not man put asunder.” (Mark 10:9)
lessons.hook: Acknowledge that divorce touches many families in the room and that this lesson is not about blaming anyone.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the difference between divorce and annulment and what the tribunal examines.

script.open: Say softly, “Many of you have family or friends affected by divorce. This is a subject that requires tenderness. We will state the Church’s teaching clearly, and also the Church’s care.” Ask, “What do you think the Church should say to a person whose marriage has ended?”
teach: Read Mark 10:2-12 and Matthew 19:3-9. Say: “The Pharisees asked about divorce. Jesus pointed back to Genesis: ‘From the beginning of creation, God made them male and female… What therefore God has joined together, let not man put asunder.’ He said that Moses allowed divorce because of hardness of heart, but ‘it was not so from the beginning.’ He taught that whoever divorces and remarries commits adultery. The Church holds that a valid, consummated sacramental marriage is indissoluble; it can be ended only by death. No power on earth, not even the Pope, can dissolve it.”

Say: “Annulment. An annulment (a declaration of nullity) is not a ‘Catholic divorce.’ It is a finding by a Church tribunal that, despite appearances, a valid marriage never existed from the beginning, because something essential was lacking at the time of the wedding. Grounds include: lack of canonical form; an impediment (such as a prior bond); lack of freedom (force or grave fear); lack of due discretion or the capacity to assume the obligations of marriage; deceit; simulation (excluding permanence, fidelity or children); condition. The process: petition to the diocesan tribunal, testimony, witnesses, review by a judge, and a defender of the bond. Pope Francis streamlined it in 2015 (Mitis Iudex). Children from an annulled marriage remain legitimate. The process can be difficult but can bring healing.”

Say: “Practical teaching. Civil divorce is sometimes tolerated as the only way to protect rights or children (CCC 2383). Separation without remarriage is allowed in cases of abuse or danger; Rita’s situation shows a dangerous marriage, and the Church does not require anyone to remain in danger. Divorced Catholics are not excommunicated and remain members. Those who have remarried without an annulment cannot receive Communion, since their situation contradicts the union of Christ and the Church, but are encouraged to attend Mass, pray, and take part in the community. Pope Francis in Amoris Laetitia (2016) asked pastors to accompany them, discern, and integrate them. Children of divorce are not at fault. The Church ministers through programs like Rachel’s Vineyard and divorce support groups. Prevention: good preparation for marriage, and support afterward.”
ask: Can the Church dissolve a valid sacramental marriage? (No.)
What is an annulment? (A declaration that a valid marriage never existed.)
May a divorced Catholic receive Communion? (Yes, unless remarried without annulment.)
practice: Make a chart: divorce vs annulment (what it is, who decides, effects).
List the main grounds for nullity.
Write a short compassionate message you would send to a friend whose parents are divorcing.
Identify one resource at your parish for those in difficult marriages.
script.close: Pray for families in pain. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for a family that is hurting.”

tryit: Distinguish annulment from divorce.
List grounds for nullity.
Describe the Church’s care for the divorced.
lessons.saintStory:
Rita was born around 1381 in Roccaporena, Italy. She wished to be a nun, but her parents arranged a marriage at twelve to Paolo, a man with a violent temper. For about eighteen years, she endured his anger and infidelity. She prayed for him and treated him with patience, and eventually he changed. Not long afterward, he was killed in a feud.
Her twin sons wanted revenge for their father’s death. Rita begged them to forgive. Fearful that they would commit murder, she prayed that God would take them before they sinned. Both sons died of illness within a year, after having reconciled.
Widowed and childless, Rita sought to join the Augustinian convent in Cascia, and was refused three times, because of the feuds in her family. She helped reconcile the families, and was admitted. She lived there forty years in prayer. A wound appeared on her forehead, from a thorn of Christ’s crown, as she prayed before a crucifix. She died in 1457. She is called the “Saint of the Impossible” and is invoked by those in difficult marriages.

lessons.title: Same-sex attraction and the Church’s teaching
lessons.idea: The Church teaches that every person has dignity and must be treated with respect, compassion and sensitivity, and that marriage is a lifelong union of one man and one woman. It calls people with same-sex attraction to chastity.
lessons.question: How can the Church say both “love everyone” and “marriage is man and woman”?
lessons.activity: Write a short guide: how to talk with a friend who is gay and a Christian.
teach: Sensitive topic: some students are living this. Teach clearly, charitably and without humiliating anyone; let students step out; never ask a student to “out” themselves.

The Catechism says homosexual persons “must be accepted with respect, compassion, and sensitivity. Every sign of unjust discrimination in their regard should be avoided” (CCC 2358). Same-sex attraction itself is not a sin. Acts are held to be contrary to the natural law (CCC 2357), and persons are called to chastity (CCC 2359).
Marriage, in Catholic teaching, is the lifelong union of a man and a woman, open to children (CCC 1601). The Church’s teaching does not allow it to bless same-sex marriage as a sacrament.

Many people find this teaching very painful. A good response listens, does not mock or condemn, and affirms that every person is made in God’s image and loved by God. Bullying has no place in a Catholic school.
talk: What does it mean to “accept with respect, compassion and sensitivity”?
