Why can disagreeing with someone’s choice still be done with love?
What would it take for a parish to feel safe for everyone?
quiz: What does CCC 2358 say about people with same-sex attraction?|They are excommunicated|They cannot be baptized|They must be treated with respect, compassion and sensitivity|They should be avoided|2|CCC 2358.
Is same-sex attraction itself a sin?|No, the Church distinguishes attraction from acts|Yes, always|The Church has no teaching|Only for clergy|0|CCC 2358–2359.
In Catholic teaching, marriage is…|Any loving relationship|A temporary contract|A matter of civil law only|A lifelong union of a man and a woman|3|CCC 1601.
lessons.life: Ask yourself: have I ever laughed at a joke that hurt someone? Choose to stop and apologize if you need to.
lessons.saint: Aelred of Rievaulx: an abbot who wrote about holy friendship.
misc: “The Church teaches that being gay is a sin.”
lessons.mem: “Love one another as I have loved you.” (John 13:34)
lessons.hook: Set ground rules: listen, no jokes, no personal questions. Let students step out. Open with the Church’s call to respect every person.
lessons.assess: Ask students to state the Church’s teaching and describe how to treat a friend with love and truth.

script.open: Say gently, “This lesson deals with a sensitive subject. In this room, everyone is to be treated with respect, whatever their experience. We will state the Church’s teaching carefully, with its call to love, and give time for questions.” Ask, “What is the difference between how the Church treats a person and what the Church teaches about acts?”
teach: Say: “The Catechism teaches (CCC 2357-2359): ‘Homosexuality refers to relations between men or between women who experience an exclusive or predominant sexual attraction toward persons of the same sex.’ Tradition, based on Scripture (Genesis 19, Romans 1:24-27, 1 Corinthians 6:9-10), has always declared that ‘homosexual acts are intrinsically disordered’ and contrary to the natural law, since they close the sexual act to the gift of life and do not proceed from a genuine complementarity. The Church distinguishes between the orientation (an inclination, not a sin) and acts. ‘The number of men and women who have deep-seated homosexual tendencies is not negligible. This inclination, which is objectively disordered, constitutes for most of them a trial.’”

Say: “Then, crucially: ‘They must be accepted with respect, compassion, and sensitivity. Every sign of unjust discrimination in their regard should be avoided.’ (CCC 2358) ‘Homosexual persons are called to chastity.’ Like all, they’re called to self-mastery, to friendship, to prayer, to the sacraments, and to Christian perfection. Pope Francis asked, ‘Who am I to judge?’ about a gay person who seeks the Lord with goodwill, and has also said the Church should welcome. The Church rejects violence and harassment against gay persons, and it’s a serious sin to treat them with contempt. Bullying is wrong. Parents should love their children whatever. The Church says that ‘God’s love is for everyone.’”

Say: “Questions arise. Why isn’t same-sex marriage recognized? Because the Church sees marriage as the union of a man and a woman, ordered to the good of the spouses and children (the complementarity of the sexes). Civil law is different from the sacrament, and the Church has asked that civil law not redefine marriage. The Church recognizes that people disagree, including many Catholics. Experiences vary: some people find the teaching hard and feel excluded. Others live it with joy: groups such as Courage offer support for chaste living. The Church acknowledges failures in the past: too often, gay people were met with cruelty. Our call: truth and love together. Practical guidance: listen, don’t assume, don’t use slurs, keep friendships, point to Christ, avoid both condemnation and dismissal of the teaching. Aelred’s ideal of friendship in Christ is available to all.”
ask: Is a homosexual orientation a sin? (No; the Church distinguishes orientation from acts.)
How should persons with same-sex attraction be treated? (With respect, compassion and sensitivity; no unjust discrimination.)
To what are they called? (Chastity, friendship, prayer, sacraments, holiness.)
practice: Write the Church’s teaching in four sentences, including both the moral teaching and the call to respect.
Draft a respectful response to a friend who says the Church hates gay people.
List what a welcoming parish does and does not do.
Share with a partner.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, help us to love everyone with truth and tenderness.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Treat everyone you meet with dignity.”

tryit: State the Church’s teaching in her own words.
Identify the three requirements of pastoral care.
Draft a respectful response to a friend.
lessons.saintStory:
Aelred was born around 1110 in northern England, to a family of priests. He grew up at the court of King David of Scotland, as a steward. He became a Cistercian monk at Rievaulx in 1134, and later abbot in 1147, leading a community of about 600 monks and lay brothers.
Aelred wrote Spiritual Friendship, based on Cicero’s dialogue On Friendship, but transformed by Christ. In it, he taught that “God is friendship.” He wrote of friendship as a path to God, grounded in a shared love of Christ. Friends aid each other in virtue and share a love of what is good. He said, “Here we are, you and I, and I hope a third, Christ, is in our midst.”
He had been tender and affectionate with his monks. He suffered from painful illness in his last years. He died in 1167. His writings show that deep friendship is a gift in the celibate life.

lessons.title: Euthanasia, suicide and caring for the dying
lessons.idea: Life is a gift to be received, so the Church rejects euthanasia and assisted suicide, yet it also does not require extraordinary treatments and strongly supports palliative care and accompaniment of the dying.
lessons.question: What is the difference between letting someone die and killing?
lessons.activity: Interview a hospice worker or read about palliative care.
teach: Sensitive topic: some students have lost a loved one to suicide or illness. Provide resources and use gentle language.

Euthanasia, acts or omissions that by their nature or intention cause death to end suffering, is morally unacceptable (CCC 2277). The Church distinguishes this from stopping treatments that are burdensome or disproportionate (CCC 2278) and from pain relief even if it shortens life (CCC 2279).

Suicide is gravely contrary to love of self and God (CCC 2280–2281), yet mental illness, fear and anguish may lessen responsibility, and “we should not despair of the eternal salvation of persons who have taken their own lives” (CCC 2282–2283).
If you or someone you know is in crisis, tell a trusted adult and call or text 988 (in the U.S.). The Church’s answer to suffering is accompaniment and care.
talk: What is the difference between refusing a burdensome treatment and killing a patient?
Why does the Church say pain relief is good?
What can a community do for someone who is dying or who feels they are a burden?
quiz: The Church teaches that euthanasia is…|A matter of choice|Only wrong for Catholics|Morally unacceptable|Required in some cases|2|CCC 2277.
Which of these is allowed?|Directly causing death to end suffering|Refusing disproportionate or burdensome treatment|Withholding food and water to cause death|Assisted suicide|1|CCC 2278.
CCC 2283 says…|Prayer for them is forbidden|Such people are certainly lost|They may not be mentioned|We should not despair of the salvation of those who have taken their own lives|3|God knows hearts.
lessons.life: Make a card for someone in a nursing home or hospice, and know the number 988.
lessons.saint: Cicely Saunders: a nurse and doctor who founded modern hospice care.
misc: “The Church says every possible medical treatment must always be used.”
“A person who dies by suicide is automatically lost forever.”
lessons.mem: “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I fear no evil, for you are with me.” (Psalm 23:4)
lessons.hook: Acknowledge that some students have lost someone. Open with a moment of silence for those who have died.
lessons.assess: Ask students to distinguish euthanasia from refusing burdensome treatment and describe good palliative care.

script.open: Be calm. Say, “This is a hard topic. Some of you may have lost someone or face illness in your family. We’ll treat it carefully.” Ask, “What matters most to a person near the end of life?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “The Church teaches that life is a gift, and we are stewards, not owners. The Catechism: ‘Euthanasia, an action or omission which of itself or by intention causes death in order that all suffering may be eliminated, is morally unacceptable.’ (CCC 2277) Euthanasia is the intentional killing of a sick or dying person. Assisted suicide is helping someone to kill themselves. Both are wrong, even with consent and even for compassion. Suicide is gravely contrary to love of self, God and neighbor. The Church recognizes that psychological disturbance, anguish or fear can diminish responsibility (CCC 2282-2283); we do not despair of the salvation of those who take their own lives, and pray for them.”

Say: “Distinctions. The Church allows, and sometimes requires, the withdrawal or refusal of treatment that is burdensome, dangerous, extraordinary or disproportionate to the expected outcome. This is not euthanasia, but acceptance of the human condition. Ordinary means, such as food, water, and basic care, must be provided unless they cannot be absorbed or cause grave burden. Pain relief, even if it might shorten life as an unintended effect, is allowed. This is the principle of double effect. Palliative care, which treats pain and symptoms, supports the whole person. Hospice affirms that dying is a natural process. Advance directives and a health care proxy are advisable, and should be consistent with Church teaching.”

Say: “Why not euthanasia? Because it treats a person’s worth as dependent on health or usefulness; because it can become pressure on the vulnerable; because it changes the practice of medicine from healing to killing; and because suffering has meaning when united with love, though we should work to relieve it. Pope John Paul II’s Evangelium Vitae: ‘Euthanasia is a grave violation of the law of God.’ Pope Francis: ‘We must accompany people towards death, but not provoke death.’ Countries that have legalized euthanasia have seen the categories expand. Care for the dying is an act of love: presence, touch, prayer, sacraments (Anointing, Viaticum), forgiveness, farewells. Saunders’s total pain approach cares for all dimensions. As the Church says, ‘Death is not the end but the doorway.’ Hope in resurrection changes how we die.”
ask: Is euthanasia acceptable? (No; the Church teaches it is morally wrong.)
May we refuse burdensome treatment? (Yes, extraordinary or disproportionate means may be refused.)
What is palliative care? (Care that relieves pain and supports the whole person.)
practice: Prepare a chart: euthanasia, refusing extraordinary treatment, palliative sedation, and hospice. Mark which are allowed and which not, and why.
Write a short explanation of ‘total pain.’
Draft a letter to a dying relative, expressing love and gratitude.
List ways to accompany the dying.
script.close: Pray for the dying: “Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask a trusted adult about your family’s wishes for care.”

tryit: Distinguish killing from allowing to die.
Distinguish ordinary from extraordinary means.
Describe good palliative care.
lessons.saintStory:
Cicely Saunders was born in 1918 in England. She trained as a nurse, then a social worker, and finally became a doctor at thirty-three. In 1948, she befriended a dying patient, David Tasma, a Polish Jewish refugee. He asked her, “I only want what is in your mind and in your heart.” He left her £500, saying, “I will be a window in your home.”
She spent years working in hospitals for the dying. She saw that patients suffered from physical pain but also from fear, loneliness and the sense of being a burden. She developed the idea of “total pain”: physical, emotional, social and spiritual. She taught regular doses of pain relief to prevent pain, rather than waiting for it to return.
In 1967 she opened St. Christopher’s Hospice in London, the first modern hospice. It became a model across the world. She said to patients, “You matter because you are you, and you matter to the end of your life. We will do all we can not only to help you die peacefully, but also to live until you die.” She was a devout Christian. She died in 2005 in her own hospice.

units.title: The Church’s rites, indulgences and funerals
units.eq: How does the Church celebrate and accompany us?

lessons.title: Rites, sacramentals and popular devotion
lessons.idea: The Church celebrates in different rites, such as the Roman, Byzantine and Armenian, and uses sacramentals such as blessings, holy water and medals to sanctify life. Popular devotion expresses the faith of the people.
lessons.question: What is the difference between a sacrament and a sacramental?
lessons.activity: Compare two rites using videos or visits. Make a chart of sacraments and sacramentals, and design a family blessing for a home or meal.
teach: The mystery of Christ is celebrated in many liturgical traditions: Roman, Byzantine, Alexandrian, Antiochene, Armenian, Chaldean and others. Unity in faith, diversity in rites (CCC 1200–1206).
Sacramentals are “sacred signs” instituted by the Church that prepare us for grace (CCC 1667–1673). Examples: blessings, holy water, ashes, candles, medals.
Popular piety includes pilgrimages, processions, the Way of the Cross and the Rosary (CCC 1674–1676). It must be guided by the liturgy and not replace it (CCC 1675).
Sacramentals are not magic. Their effect depends on faith and the Church’s prayer (CCC 1670).
talk: What sacramentals are in your home?
What does diversity of rites teach about the Church?
How do devotions lead us to the sacraments?
quiz: A sacramental is…|A sacred sign instituted by the Church|A sacrament|A superstition|A prayer book|0|CCC 1667.
Examples of sacramentals include…|Marriage|Holy water and blessings|Eucharist|Baptism|1|CCC 1668.
Popular piety should…|Be guided by the liturgy|Replace Mass|Be ignored|Be hidden|0|CCC 1675.
lessons.life: Bless your home or a meal this week, and learn the meaning of a sacramental you own.
lessons.saint: Simon Stock: a Carmelite associated by tradition with the brown scapular.
lessons.mem: “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you.” (Psalm 141:2)
lessons.hook: Show holy water, a medal, a rosary and ashes. Ask which are sacraments and which are not.
lessons.assess: Ask students to distinguish sacrament, sacramental and devotion with examples.

script.open: Hold up some items: holy water, a rosary, a medal, a candle. Ask, “Are these sacraments? What are they? Why do Catholics use them?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Sacramentals are ‘sacred signs which bear a certain resemblance to the sacraments, and by which spiritual effects are signified and obtained through the intercession of the Church.’ (CCC 1667) Unlike the sacraments, they were instituted by the Church, not Christ; they don’t confer sanctifying grace ex opere operato, but prepare us to receive it and dispose us to cooperate. Their effect depends on the faith of the user. Types: blessings (of persons, meals, objects, places), consecrations and dedications, exorcisms. Objects: holy water, blessed salt, ashes, palms, candles, rosaries, medals, scapulars, crucifixes, statues, icons, relics. Actions: Sign of the Cross, genuflection, processions, pilgrimages.”

Say: “Why do we use them? We are embodied, and God used material things in the Incarnation. They remind us of God’s presence and sanctify the daily life. Holy water recalls Baptism. Ashes: we are dust. Candles: Christ the Light. Incense: prayer rising. They can be misused: superstition, treating them as lucky charms. The Church guards against both neglect and abuse. A blessing is a prayer calling God’s favor. The ordinary ministers are priests and deacons, but laypeople can give some blessings (parents blessing children). The Roman Ritual contains the Book of Blessings. Exorcism is a particular kind of sacramental for people possessed by demons; a major exorcism is allowed only by a priest with the bishop’s permission.”

Say: “Popular piety. The Church values devotions as a way the faith takes root in cultures: the Rosary, Stations of the Cross, novenas, Eucharistic Adoration, Benediction, Divine Mercy chaplet, litanies, pilgrimages (Lourdes, Fatima, Guadalupe, Walsingham, Compostela), processions (Corpus Christi, Good Friday), shrines, Marian apparitions, the Sacred Heart, first Fridays, May crowning, and parish festivals. The Directory on Popular Piety (2001) says they must be in harmony with the liturgy, which is the source and summit. Devotions are optional; the liturgy has priority. They should be Christ-centered, rooted in Scripture and the Church’s teaching. The brown scapular reminds the wearer to follow Mary’s example, not a guarantee of salvation without conversion.”
ask: What is a sacramental? (A sacred sign instituted by the Church that prepares us for grace.)
How do sacramentals differ from sacraments? (They don’t work ex opere operato; their effect depends on faith.)
How should popular devotions relate to liturgy? (In harmony with it; liturgy has priority.)
practice: Make a three-column table: Sacraments / Sacramentals / Devotions, with ten examples.
For each sacramental, write the sacrament it recalls.
Identify one devotion you want to practice more.
Write a short guide on how to use sacramentals rightly and avoid superstition.
script.close: Bless each other with holy water. Pray a Hail Mary. Send home: “Use a sacramental with intention this week.”

tryit: Sort items into sacraments, sacramentals and devotions.
Say what each does.
Explain how to use them rightly.
lessons.saintStory:
Simon Stock is a figure whose life is mostly known through legend. He was an Englishman who is said to have lived as a hermit in the hollow of a tree (hence “Stock”), before joining the Carmelites, who had been driven out of the Holy Land. He became their superior general around 1247 and helped adapt their rule for a life in Europe.
According to tradition, on July 16, 1251, in Cambridge, he was praying to Mary for help for his order, which was in difficulty. She appeared to him holding the brown scapular, a piece of cloth worn over the shoulders, saying, “Receive, my beloved son, this scapular of thy order; it is the badge of my confraternity, a privilege for thee and for all Carmelites. Whoever dies clothed in this shall not suffer eternal fire.”
Historians question the details, but the devotion to the scapular grew. The Church teaches it is a sacramental: a sign of consecration to Mary and a reminder to live the Gospel. It is not a magic charm. He died in 1265.

lessons.title: Indulgences, purgatory and the communion of saints
lessons.idea: An indulgence is the Church’s way of applying Christ’s mercy to remove the temporal punishment due to sin already forgiven. It rests on the communion of saints and requires conversion, Confession, Communion and prayer.
lessons.question: What is an indulgence and what is it not?
lessons.activity: Study a table of indulgences (partial and plenary). Write a short answer to “Can you buy forgiveness?” using the Catechism, then plan how to gain a plenary indulgence.
teach: Sin has two consequences: eternal (removed by forgiveness) and temporal (the need for purification) (CCC 1472–1473). Indulgences remit temporal punishment (CCC 1471).

Rooted in the communion of saints: the Church draws on the “treasury” of Christ’s and the saints’ merits (CCC 1475–1477). Conditions: the sacrament of Penance, Communion, prayer for the pope’s intentions, detachment from sin (CCC 1471–1479).
Indulgences cannot be bought; the sale of indulgences was an abuse condemned at Trent and abolished by Pius V (1567). Indulgences can be gained for oneself or for the dead (CCC 1498).
Link to purgatory (CCC 1030–1032) and to prayer for the dead (2 Maccabees 12:44–46).
talk: Why is forgiveness not the same as healing?
How can we help the dead?
Why was the sale of indulgences such a scandal?
quiz: An indulgence remits…|The guilt of sin|Nothing|Original sin|Temporal punishment for forgiven sin|3|CCC 1471.
A plenary indulgence requires…|Money|A trip|Nothing|Confession, Communion, prayer for the pope’s intentions|3|CCC 1471.
Selling indulgences was…|A custom|A command|An abuse|A sacrament|2|Trent.
lessons.life: Offer a prayer or Mass for someone who has died, and gain a plenary indulgence on All Souls with the usual conditions.
lessons.saint: Odilo of Cluny: the abbot who started the Commemoration of All Souls.
lessons.mem: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven.” (Matthew 18:18)
lessons.hook: Break a vase and glue it. Say that forgiveness mends the relationship, but cracks remain and need healing. Introduce temporal punishment.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain indulgences, the conditions and the abuse that was condemned.

script.open: Ask, “Why do Catholics pray for the dead? Where do you think a person goes who dies loving God but is not yet perfect?” Take answers.
teach: Say: “Purgatory is the final purification of those who die in God’s grace and friendship but are still imperfectly purified. They are assured of heaven, but must undergo purification to achieve the holiness needed to enter. The Catechism: CCC 1030-1032. The doctrine was defined at the Councils of Lyon II (1274), Florence (1439) and Trent (1563). Scriptural roots: 2 Maccabees 12:41-46 (Judas Maccabeus prays for the dead and offers sacrifice for their sins); 1 Corinthians 3:11-15 (a person’s work tested ‘as through fire’); Matthew 12:32 (sin forgiven ‘in the age to come’); Revelation 21:27 (nothing unclean shall enter heaven). The Fathers, including Augustine, Monica’s request, and inscriptions in the catacombs, show prayers for the dead from the earliest times.”

Say: “Purgatory is not ‘second chance’ or a mini-hell. It is a process of love: the soul’s purification, a pain of longing. Catherine of Genoa described it as the soul so full of desire to be with God that it wants to be cleansed. The ‘fire’ is the fire of love. The Church doesn’t define the details (location, time, nature of the fire). We can help the souls in purgatory by prayer, Mass, almsgiving and indulgences. November is the month of the Holy Souls. This is the communion of saints: the Church on earth helps the Church suffering.”

Say: “Indulgences. After sin is forgiven in Confession, there remains temporal punishment: the harm done to oneself and others, and the need for purification. An indulgence is ‘a remission before God of the temporal punishment due to sins whose guilt has already been forgiven, which the faithful Christian who is duly disposed gains under certain prescribed conditions through the help of the Church.’ (CCC 1471) It draws on the treasury of merits of Christ and the saints. Partial indulgences remit part; plenary indulgences remit all. Conditions for a plenary: being in a state of grace, detachment from all sin including venial, sacramental Confession (within about 20 days before or after), Communion, prayer for the Pope’s intentions, and the indulgenced work (such as a Eucharistic adoration of half an hour, praying the Rosary in a church or family, Stations of the Cross, reading Scripture for half an hour). An indulgence can be applied to oneself or to the dead. Abuses: the sale of indulgences in the 1500s, one trigger of the Reformation; Pius V in 1567 abolished indulgences linked to money. Indulgences can’t be bought.”
ask: What is purgatory? (Final purification of those who die in grace but imperfectly purified.)
What is an indulgence? (Remission of temporal punishment for sins already forgiven.)
Can indulgences be bought? (No; selling them was abolished.)
practice: Make a chart: purgatory (Scripture, Fathers, councils, what it is and is not).
List the conditions for a plenary indulgence and an act you could do.
Write a prayer for the dead, naming someone.
Plan to go to Mass on All Souls’ Day.
script.close: Pray the Eternal Rest prayer. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for a deceased relative by name.”

tryit: Explain purgatory from Scripture and reason.
Explain what an indulgence is and is not.
List the conditions for a plenary indulgence.
lessons.saintStory:
Odilo was born around 962 in the Auvergne in France to a noble family. He joined the abbey of Cluny, and became its abbot in 994, guiding it for over fifty years. Cluny at that time was the greatest monastery in Europe, with hundreds of daughter houses.
Odilo was known for gentleness and generosity. During the famine of 1033 he used the monastery’s treasures to feed the starving and sold sacred vessels to help them. He promoted the “Peace of God” movement, which tried to protect civilians and clergy from violence. He also helped buy back captives.
Around 998, he established that the monks of Cluny should pray and offer Mass for all the faithful departed on November 2, the day after All Saints. The custom spread to the whole Church and became the Commemoration of All Souls. He died in 1049, in his eighties, on a journey. He showed that love for the dead is part of love for the living.

lessons.title: Christian death and the funeral rites
lessons.idea: The Church accompanies the dying and the dead with prayer, the sacraments and the funeral Mass. The funeral rites entrust the person to God’s mercy and comfort the grieving with the hope of resurrection.
lessons.question: How does the Church help us at death?
lessons.activity: Study the Order of Christian Funerals: vigil, Mass and committal. Write the readings and prayers you would choose, and a letter of condolence.
teach: Death is the end of earthly life, and for those who die in Christ a passing into eternal life (CCC 1010–1014). “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21).
The funeral has three stations: vigil (wake), funeral Mass, and committal (CCC 1680–1690). The Mass offers the Eucharist for the deceased and entrusts them to God’s mercy.
The Church prefers burial and permits cremation if it is not chosen to deny the resurrection; ashes should be buried or entombed, not scattered (CCC 2300; Ad resurgendum cum Christo, 2016).
The rites also comfort those who mourn (CCC 1687–1690). Pray for the dead and visit the bereaved.
talk: What do the white vestments at funerals proclaim?
How can we comfort people who grieve?
Why does the Church bury or entomb ashes?
quiz: The funeral Mass offers…|A sermon about money|A party|The Eucharist for the deceased|A speech only|2|CCC 1689.
The Church recommends that cremated remains be…|Buried or entombed|Scattered|Divided|Kept at home|0|Ad resurgendum cum Christo.
The Christian hope at death is…|Fear|Reincarnation|Resurrection|Nothing|2|CCC 1012.
lessons.life: Visit a grave, pray for someone who died and write a note to someone grieving.
lessons.saint: Macrina the Younger: a sister and teacher whose dying prayer her brother recorded.
misc: “Funerals are only a celebration of the person’s life.”
lessons.mem: “I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live.” (John 11:25)
lessons.hook: Pause for a moment of silence for someone who has died. Ask: “What helped you most when someone you loved died?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the funeral rites and the Church’s teaching on cremation.

script.open: Ask, “How do other cultures treat the dead? What do you think a funeral is for?” Take answers. “The Church has a rich tradition. It teaches us how to grieve with hope.”
teach: Say: “Christians face death with hope, but also sorrow. The Catechism: ‘Death is the end of man’s earthly pilgrimage… Death is transformed by Christ.’ Jesus wept at Lazarus’s tomb. Paul writes: ‘We would not have you ignorant, brethren, concerning those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.’ (1 Thessalonians 4:13) The Church’s funeral rites express faith in the Resurrection, pray for the deceased, and comfort the living. The Order of Christian Funerals has three stages. Vigil (wake): prayers, the Liturgy of the Word, the family gathers, eulogies may be given here. Funeral Liturgy: usually a Mass, with the body present; the casket is sprinkled with holy water (a baptismal reminder) and covered with a white pall; the Easter candle; incense; the homily preaches hope, not a eulogy; the Final Commendation and Farewell.”

Say: “Committal: the rite at the grave or place of final disposition, with prayers asking for the deceased’s resurrection. The colors: white or purple; black is allowed. The funeral Mass uses prayers for the dead: ‘Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them.’ Burial in the ground is the preferred practice; the Church also permits cremation (Ad Resurgendum cum Christo, 2016), provided it is not chosen for reasons contrary to Christian faith. The ashes should be buried or entombed in a cemetery or sacred place, not scattered or kept at home, and not divided. Reasons: reverence for the body, a temple of the Spirit, destined for resurrection. Funeral rites are denied only to manifest apostates, or those who publicly refuse them, and in doubtful cases the pastor decides.”

Say: “Support for the dying and the grieving. Before death: Anointing, Viaticum (Communion as ‘food for the journey’), the Commendation of the Dying, and prayers (the Litany, the Rosary). After: prayers for the deceased, Masses, visiting the grieving, preparing meals, listening. Grief is natural and takes time. The Church offers bereavement ministries. It encourages remembering the dead in November, visiting cemeteries, and praying. Macrina’s death shows trust: Christ has conquered death. Memento mori: remembering death helps us live well (Psalm 90:12). Life’s last things: death, judgment, heaven, hell. We prepare by living in the state of grace, making our wishes known, and writing wills. Praying the Hail Mary daily: ‘pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death.’”
ask: What are the three stages of the Christian funeral? (Vigil, funeral liturgy, committal.)
What does the Church teach about cremation? (Permitted, but ashes should be buried or entombed, not scattered.)
Why is the homily at a funeral not a eulogy? (It proclaims the hope of the Resurrection.)
practice: Make a timeline of a Catholic funeral with the rites and symbols: wake, procession, holy water, pall, Easter candle, incense, commendation, committal.
Beside each, write its meaning and baptismal connection.
Write the Scripture readings and hymns you would choose for your own funeral, and why.
Write a short prayer for your family at your death.
script.close: Pray the Eternal Rest prayer and a Hail Mary. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Visit a cemetery and pray for the dead.”

tryit: Map the stages of the Christian funeral.
Match each to a meaning.
Write a prayer you would want at your funeral.
lessons.saintStory:
Macrina was born around 327 in Cappadocia, the oldest of ten children. Her family included Basil the Great, Gregory of Nyssa and Peter of Sebaste. She was engaged young, but when her fiancé died, she decided to remain unmarried, consecrated to God. She helped raise her younger brothers, including Basil, and taught them. When her father died, she persuaded her mother Emmelia to turn their estate into a monastic community where women and men lived simply, sharing work and prayer.
She supported Basil’s turn to monastic life. In 379, her brother Gregory visited her as she was dying. He wrote about her in The Life of Macrina. She lay on the floor on a rough board, with her last strength. She prayed in thanksgiving: “You, Lord, have freed us from the fear of death. You have made the end of this life the beginning of true life for us.”
She made the Sign of the Cross, whispered a final prayer, and died. Gregory describes preparing her body and her funeral. She was buried beside her parents. Her story shows a Christian death.
